2.1 Read a photographed page
Method | Acquisition orientation segmentation reading and naming
OpenCV obtains camera frames. Pillow opens image files and applies EXIF orientation; a configured
quarter turn is a camera mounting hint. The segmenter’s axis score compares empty-row evidence in
two orientations. SegmentLines(page, mergeValley=None) then estimates illumination, deskews,
filters structures/components, finds line centres, optimises seams, refines ownership and builds full-
resolution crops. Its current signature does not take a timer; the server times this complete call as
one stage.
The reader probes up to three sampled lines in both directions to resolve 180-degree inversion. The
comparison uses mean best-frame log score, not a transcript likelihood. Chosen probe outputs are
reused; remaining lines are eligible for lineworker mapping. If inversion wins, crop rotation and line
order are changed together. Metadata is reordered to match the returned text.
Each surviving crop is named with the configured writer model. A weighted arithmetic average of
class vectors supplies the page decision, with weight equal to the crop’s count of pixels below 128.
More dark pixels are treated as more evidence; the procedure is not a Bayesian multiplication of
independent observations. Supplied expected text/author are used for reported evaluation, not as
substitutes for the network prediction.

2.5 Independent line processes and numerical threads
Purpose | Parallelise independent work without confusing it with a new model
The new web/lineworkers.py stores configured reader/namer objects in parent state. When os.fork
exists and enough jobs remain, Map creates an explicit fork pool, preserving returned job order.
LINE_WORKERS=1 disables the pool; zero requests up to the CPU count, bounded by job count.
The minimum is four jobs per Map call, not necessarily four original page lines after orientation
probes have already been read.
Justification | Parallel speed depends on overhead and oversubscription
If N independent passes costt each, an ideal pool withP equal workers would take about⌈N/P⌉t
plus setup and communication. For a serial fractions, idealised Amdahl speedup is1/[s + (1−s )/P ].
These are explanatory bounds under simplified assumptions, not measured ODROID gains. Memory
bandwidth, heterogeneous cores, crop transfer, pool startup and native numerical threads alter the
outcome.
Workers attempt to cap OpenBLAS threads to one using environment settings and selected shared-
library entry points. It is best effort, not a portable proof that every backend is capped. Fork provides
copy-on-write address spaces, not zero allocation or zero IPC. The explicit fork context is distinct from
Python’s platform/version default. Forking a threaded service with native state requires deployment
care. Exceptions in pool work fall back to serial execution of the same function; errors can still
propagate if the serial function also fails [1, 2].
2.6 Dependencies and fair library comparisons
Library | First principles does not mean no libraries are present
The numerical core uses NumPy arrays and compiled linear algebra. Flask/CORS serve requests,
Pillow decodes/encodes and renders UI artefacts, OpenCV acquires camera frames, gpiod accesses
GPIO, and Python multiprocessing manages workers. Training also contains explicit PNG/JPEG
decoders. This boundary is more precise than the old manual’s blanket no-library statement.
Compare an operation with fixed inputs, parameters, dtype, padding, axes, normalisation and
reduction before comparing independently trained accuracy. A library may offer compiled/fused
kernels or GPU execution, while the custom code exposes intermediates and design rules. It is
not defensible to attach an unmeasured universal speed multiplier or accuracy gain to the word
library. Library APIs documented here were consulted for semantics; their versions are not evidence
of packages installed on the ODROID.

Purpose | What it is for
Finds one writer’s pages and pairs each with its transcript. Every stage that needs real handwriting
with known text starts here: training, profile building, and the measurement of segmentation accuracy.
Justification | Why the order matters
Several measurement scripts pair the n-th detected line crop on a page with the n-th line of that
page’s transcript. If the pages were returned in whatever order the file system happened to supply,
that pairing would still appear to work but would sometimes be comparing a line against the wrong
label, and the resulting accuracy would be wrong in a way that no error message would reveal. Sorting
makes the order a property of the filenames rather than of the file system.
Justification | Why a generator
A generator produces its values one at a time as they are asked for, rather than building the whole
list first. Here that means a caller can begin processing the first page immediately, and can stop after
one page without the cost of listing them all.

5.1 Expanded reasoning: page-to-line segmentation
5.1.1 The measurement model and why normalise lighting
The input is a grey imageG(y,x ), with rowy increasing downwards and columnxincreasing rightwards.
A pixel is an area sample, not a physical point. A useful approximate model isG =LRs +η: L is
slowly varying illumination,Rs surface reflectance andη sensor/readout noise. Paper and ink have
different reflectance. The method estimates the local paper levelBr and divides by it. IfBr≃LR paper,
then G/Br≃R s/Rpaper and the multiplicative illumination approximately cancels. This algebra is
the reason for using a ratio rather than a fixed grey threshold; it is not proof that strong shadows or
glare are removed. Additive glare, saturation, texture and a window mostly filled with ink violate the
approximation. Sauvola’s local mean/variance threshold is a published alternative [7]; choosing it
would change the measurement model and require independent comparison.
Method | Window size and edges.
A window must be wider than an individual stroke so that it estimates paper rather than that stroke,
yet narrower than the illumination variation it is supposed to track. Too small a window follows and
cancels ink; too large a window misses local shadows. Edge replication extends the nearest edge pixel
outside the image. Zero padding would invent black borders. Reflection and reduced edge windows
are alternatives. The selected radius is an implementation setting, not a universal imaging constant.

5.1.8 Complete algorithm, alternatives and verification meaning
The conceptual order is: decode greyscale; reduce the working resolution; estimate background and ink;
choose quarter-turn and fine skew; estimate pitch; remove eligible long marks; re-estimate pitch and
centres; close a mask for seam costs; compute and backtrack boundaries; assign initial bands; refine
ownership using raw and closed components; crop each line from the grey image; exclude neighbouring

preserve the mapping back to the original pixels used for glyph extraction.

labelled boundaries and another trained model. Seams offer explicit, inspectable geometry. That is a
defensible method trade-off, not proof of superiority on every page.
Verification asks whether sums, rotations, DP recurrence and ownership obey their definitions.
Validation asks whether the resulting lines contain the intended handwriting under the photographed

path in a low-cost valley explains the optimisation; only comparison with labelled ink establishes

4 the running totals are 2, 5, 6, 10, and the sum of the middle two numbers is 6 minus 2, which is 4.
No addition is needed at query time, however long the stretch.

corrupt every rectangle total computed from that part of the table. Using 64-bit floating point avoids
this with room to spare.

Method | How it works
The four corner positions of every pixel’s window are built as whole arrays of indices rather than
being computed one pixel at a time, and the table is then read at all of them simultaneously. The
result is the same four-term expression as before, evaluated for the entire image in a handful of array
operations.
Doing it this way rather than with a loop matters because the loop would run in the Python interpreter,
which is roughly two orders of magnitude slower than the same arithmetic performed inside numpy’s
compiled code. For a multi-megapixel photograph that is the difference between a fraction of a second
and several minutes.
Method | What happens at the edges
A window centred near the border of the image hangs off the edge. The corner indices are clipped to
stay inside the array, so the window is effectively cut short and the total covers fewer pixels than it
would in the middle of the image. That is not corrected here, because the correction depends on what
the caller wants:BoxMean divides by the number of pixels actually covered, whileErode compares
against that same count. Both get what they need fromBoxCount.

The count is the clipped height of the window multiplied by its clipped width. Because those two

misbehave in a band around the whole page.

sum against this count. Comparing against the nominal area instead would make the test
impossible to satisfy anywhere near the border, and a band around the page would be eroded

Method | Background: what morphology is
Morphology is the family of operations that change the shapes in a mask rather than the values in an
image. The two basic operations are growing a shape outwards and shrinking it inwards, and almost
everything else is built by combining them. The window they look through is called the structuring
element; here it is always a square.

Growing shapes is used in this pipeline to make separate pieces of ink touch, so that they can be
treated as one object. The clearest example is a letter such as i or j, which is written as two separate
marks: growing both slightly makes them touch, after which the grouping stage treats the letter and
its dot as a single piece and cannot assign them to different lines of writing.

the gap: once two sides have been joined, eroding the joined shape thins it but does not split it again.

boundary and the last run of a row is always closed before the next row’s first run begins.

and the answer is returned as the value at the centre of the chosen bin rather than as a bin number.

Purpose | What it is for
This is the first real decision in the whole pipeline: for every pixel of the photograph, is this pen or
is this paper? Everything downstream, from finding the lines to cutting out letters, works on the
answer. Getting it wrong in one direction loses strokes; getting it wrong in the other fills the page
with shadows and paper texture that then get mistaken for writing.
Justification | Background: why a single threshold is not enough
The obvious method is a global threshold: pick one grey value, call everything darker than it ink.
That works for a scanner, where the lamp lights the page evenly. It fails badly for a photograph taken
with a phone, because the illumination is not even. One corner of the page sits under a lamp and the
opposite corner sits in shadow, and the page is often slightly curved so the middle is brighter than
the edges. The result is that paper in the bright corner can be lighter than 220 while paper in the
shadowed corner is darker than 150, and real pen ink in the bright corner is around 90. There is no
single number that separates ink from paper everywhere at once: any threshold low enough to reject
the shadowed paper also rejects the pale pen strokes, and any threshold high enough to catch the
pale strokes also catches the shadow.
Method | The idea: divide out the illumination
The fix is to stop asking "is this pixel dark?" and ask instead "is this pixel darker than the paper
immediately around it?". The illumination varies smoothly across the page, so over a small neigh-
bourhood it is almost constant. If the brightness of a pixel is modelled as the true reflectance of the
page at that point multiplied by the local illumination, then dividing by an estimate of that local
illumination cancels it and leaves the reflectance, which is the thing that actually distinguishes pen
from paper.

The method rests on one observation: of everything in the frame, the sheet of paper is both bright
and large. The desk may be bright too, but it surrounds the page rather than forming one solid
region with it, because a visible dark rim separates them, which is the shadow the sheet casts and the
contrast at its cut edge. So the paper is the largestconnectedbright region, where connected means
one can walk from any pixel of it to any other without leaving it.

The search is done on a copy of the page reduced by a factor of four in each direction, by averaging
each 4 by 4 block of pixels into one. Two reasons. Speed: a sixteenth of the pixels means a sixteenth

suppresses noise and small features, so the result is dominated by the large-scale structure, which is
what is being looked for. The reduction uses a block average rather than taking every fourth pixel,
because taking every fourth pixel can land entirely in a gap and miss a thin dark rim completely,
whereas an average over the block always registers it.

grey level out of 255, while the other plausible convention differed by up to 245 along the edges. A
difference of that size is not a rounding detail, it is a row of pixels in the wrong place.

Method | The principle: concentration
Consider the row profile again, the count of ink pixels per row. When the page is level, every letter on
a line contributes to the same few rows, so those rows have very large counts and the rows between
lines have almost none. When the page is tilted, the left end of a line sits higher than the right end,
so the same ink is spread over many more rows, each with a smaller count. The total amount of ink
is identical either way, since rotating the page does not create or destroy pixels. What changes is how

all that is needed is a number that measures concentration.

quadruples its contribution. So for a fixed total, the sum of squares is largest when the total is piled
into as few entries as possible and smallest when it is spread evenly.

angle offered. The code instead shifts the indices so the smallest becomes zero, which keeps every
pixel in its own distinct row and lets the profile grow as tall as it needs to be.

Clipping an index is usually the safe thing to do; here it silently converts a correct measurement
into one that is guaranteed to give the wrong answer.

those ties in favour of going straight, so that the seam moves only when moving buys it something,
namely avoiding ink. At 0.02 per row it is far smaller than the cost of crossing a stroke, so it never
persuades the seam to cut through a letter in order to stay level; it only decides between routes that
are otherwise equivalent. This is aregularisationterm, which is the general name for a small extra
cost added to express a preference among solutions that the main objective cannot distinguish.
Method | Recovering the path
The accumulated cost gives the price of the best seam but not its route, so as each cell is filled the
winning move is recorded in a second array. When the pass is complete, the lowest value in the final
column is the end of the best seam, and following the stored moves backwards from there reconstructs
the whole path, column by column, right to left. This isbacktracking, and it is the standard
companion to dynamic programming: the forward pass computes the value of the best solution, the
backward pass reads off what that solution actually was.
Method | How it is made fast in practice
Written as a loop over rows inside a loop over columns this would be slow in Python. Instead, for
each column, the candidate costs from all 2·step+1 possible moves are formed as whole shifted copies
of the previous column, stacked into a small array, and the minimum is taken down the stack in one
operation. Shifting a column by d rows and adding the penalty handles every row’s d-th candidate
at once. Only the loop over columns remains in Python, because columns are genuinely sequential:
column x cannot be computed before column x−1.
The shifted copies are filled with infinity where the shift runs off the end of the array. Infinity is
the natural value for an impossible move, because taking a minimum automatically never selects it,
with no need for a special case in the code.

stroke, and the midline term only ever acts as a tie-breaker. Expressing the displacement in units of
the half-gap rather than in pixels keeps that balance the same for widely and narrowly spaced writing.

Method | Closing the mask first
The mask is closed, dilated then eroded by about 0.07 pitches, before being used as cost. The reason
is a specific failure mode: handwriting has narrow gaps inside it, between the two strokes of an n or
where a pen lifted, and a seam is happy to thread through such a gap, because threading it is free
while going round costs ink. The cut then passes through the middle of a letter. Closing fills gaps
narrower than the structuring element while leaving the outer shape of the stroke nearly unchanged,
so the threading routes disappear but the cut still traces the true outline of the letter.
Closing rather than plain dilation is the point. Dilation alone would also close the gaps, but it would
leave every stroke thickened by the full radius, and the cut would then trace a bloated blob standing
well clear of the real ink, wasting vertical space in both crops. The erosion that follows the dilation
undoes the thickening in the places where it was not needed, which is exactly the property that
distinguishes a closing from a dilation.
Evidence | The step limit
The seam here is allowed 7 rows of vertical movement per column, against the default of 3. A tall
narrow descender, such as the tail of a y, demands a sharp deflection: the cut must drop below the
tail and climb back within the few columns the tail occupies. With a small step limit the cut simply
cannot turn fast enough and is forced through the tail. The cost of the larger limit is a little more
work per pixel and a little more freedom to wander, the latter being what the midline penalty is there
to restrain.
Method | The outer boundaries
Cuts exist only between consecutive centres, so the first line has no cut above it and the last none
below. Two straight boundaries are added at 0.75 pitches beyond the outermost centres, clipped
to the page. They are straight because there is no second line on the far side to avoid, so there is
nothing for a seam to dodge, and 0.75 pitches is enough to clear the ascenders of the first line and the
descenders of the last. The number of bands is then one less than the number of boundaries, which is
why L is computed that way.

Purpose | What it is for
A sheet of lined or gridded paper carries printing that was never written by hand: the ruled lines, the
red margin line, the holes and the darkened spine where the page meets the binding. All of it is ink
as far as the mask is concerned, and all of it is poison for the stages that follow. A ruled line runs
the full width of the page, so it joins every letter on a line into one connected blob, which destroys
the per-letter analysis that the cutter depends on, and it adds a huge horizontal stroke to every row
profile. This function removes that printing while leaving the writing intact.
Method | The distinguishing property: length
The property that separates printing from writing is not darkness, since a ruled line can be as dark as
a pencil stroke, and not thickness, since both are a pen’s width. It islength. A ruled line crosses the
whole page in one unbroken straight run. Handwriting contains straight pieces too, but short ones:
the longest horizontal stroke in ordinary writing is the crossbar of a t or the join between two letters,
neither more than a fraction of a line’s height. So a threshold on run length, expressed in line pitches,
separates the two reliably.

⌊·⌋rounding down to a whole number of pixels
The threshold of 1.25 pitches sits in a wide gap. A ruled line is tens of pitches long, and the longest
horizontal stroke in handwriting is well under one pitch, since a letter is about half a pitch wide.
Anything between about 1 and several pitches would give the same result, so the exact figure is not
delicate. The vertical direction gets 1.4 pitches, slightly more, because a tall letter like a capital L or
an f with a long descender genuinely can run more than a pitch vertically, and the extra margin keeps
such letters out of the deletion.
Method | Tolerating a tilt
A ruled line on a page that is still a fraction of a degree off level is not a single row of pixels. It drifts
downward as it crosses the page, so any one row contains only the piece of it that happens to lie in
that row, and a run-length test applied row by row sees a series of short runs rather than one long
one, and deletes nothing. The fix is to dilate the mask by one pixel vertically before the test, so that
each row contains the line’s pixels from the rows immediately above and below as well and the run
becomes unbroken again.
But dilating also thickens the writing, and a test applied to a thickened mask would mark pixels
that were never ink. So the result is dilated back and then intersected with the original mask, which
restricts the deletion to pixels that really were ink to begin with. In morphological terms the sequence
dilate, test, dilate, intersect is a closing used as a detector rather than as a filter: the dilation makes
the feature visible to the test, and the intersection confines the consequences to the original shape.
The vertical pass uses a radius of 3 rather than 1 because the structures it targets, the shadow at the
spine of a notebook and the edge of the sheet, are not straight. They wobble by several pixels across
the height of the page, so a tolerance of one pixel is not enough to make them read as one continuous
run.
Method | Masking off the surround first
Before any of this, PaperRegionMask locates the sheet and everything outside it is deleted from the
mask in one intersection. This is done first because it is the cheapest and most decisive filter available:
the desk, the hand and the shadow beyond the page account for a large share of the false ink on a
photograph, and removing them wholesale means the subtler tests that follow are not distracted by
them.
Justification | What is returned, and why the counts
Besides the cleaned mask, the function returns the pitch and the paper mask, both already computed
here and needed later, and two counts: how many ink pixels lay outside the paper and how many
were deleted as printed structure. The counts feed the diagnostics dictionary that SegmentLines
returns. They exist because a failure of this stage is otherwise invisible: if the paper mask is wrong,
the ink-outside-paper count is enormous, and if the run-length thresholds are wrong for a given page,
the removed-pixel count is far larger or smaller than expected. Reporting them makes a silent failure
a visible one.

piece in another band is that band’s own writing.

misplaced piece among the neighbours would drag a mean, while the median reports where the bulk
of the line actually is.

Method | The dot rule
The last and most specific correction handles the dots of i and j. A dot floats clear of its own letter,
often nearer to the line above than to its own line’s body, so neither the band nor a nearest-centre
test places it reliably. What does place it is the letter underneath it.
A piece is a dot candidate when it is small, under 0.1 P2, compact, no more than 0.45 pitches in either
direction, and roughly round, its longer side no more than 2.2 times its shorter. The roundness test is
what excludes a comma or an accent from being treated as a dot. The rows below the candidate are
then scanned, up to 0.4 pitches down, for the first substantial piece appearing beneath it, and the dot
is given to that piece’s line, provided the geometry agrees: the line’s writing must sit between 0.25
and 0.7 pitches below the dot, which is where a dot floats above its own line’s body. That final check
is what stops the rule firing when the piece found below happens to belong to a line further away.

All of this produces, for each piece, either a band index or a marker meaning discard. The ownership
array is then filled in one operation: a pixel takes its piece’s assigned band if the piece was one of those
the rules relocated, and its own band index otherwise. A copy is kept before the later corrections run,
because those corrections need to know which pixels were already moved here, in order not to undo
that work.

Purpose | The problem it solves
This is the mirror image of the previous correction. There, a dot on the lower line was welded to a
descender from above and wrongly given to the upper line. Here the welding runs the other way: a
small ring-shaped mark belonging to the lower line, such as the dot of an i written as a small circle,
or the loop at the top of a letter, is fused to the stem it sits on, and the stem’s line is the one it
should follow. The two corrections exist separately because the evidence needed differs: finding a ring
requires detecting a hole, which the dot rule does not do.
Method | Finding a candidate: walking up from the bottom
The candidate is not a whole component here but a part of one, so it cannot be found by labelling. It
is found geometrically. For each component, the lowest ink pixel in each column is located, and those
bottom points are examined in order from the lowest upward, since the ring sits at the top of a stem
and the stem’s foot is the lowest point of the structure.

From each bottom point the algorithm walks upward, measuring at every row how wide the component
is within a window around the column, and tracking the widest it has been. The walk stops when the
width drops below 45 percent of that maximum. That point is the junction between the blob and
the stem: a ring is wide, the stem below it is narrow, so the width collapses exactly where one ends
and the other begins. This is a one-dimensional version of a shape-decomposition idea that recurs in
image analysis: a narrow neck is where an object naturally divides.
Method | Validating the shape
Three conditions must hold before the candidate is accepted as a ring.
•Its width is between 0.2 and 0.45 pitches.Narrower is a stroke, wider is a letter body.
• It is roughly as tall as it is wide,with a height-to-width ratio between 0.6 and 1.6. A ring
is round; a stroke is not.
• It encloses a hole.This is the decisive test, and it is carried out by labelling the components
of the inverse of the blob after padding it with a border. If the blob encloses a hole then the
background splits into two components, the outside and the hole, so a count of fewer than two
components means there is no hole and the candidate is a hook or a curl rather than a ring.
The padding before that test is not optional. Without a border of background all round, a blob
touching the edge of the extracted window would let the outside connect to the hole along that edge,
merging them into one component and hiding the hole. Padding guarantees the outside is a single
region that surrounds the blob completely. Counting holes by labelling the background is a standard
technique, and the number it yields is related to theEuler numberof the shape, the classical
topological measure of components minus holes.
Method | The decision
As before, the first other piece appearing below the ring identifies the line to move to, the two bands
must be adjacent, the closed component must not be large enough to be a whole word, and the
junction must lie no more than 0.45 pitches above the target line’s centre. Only the ring’s own pixels
are reassigned, confined to the rows between the junction and the bottom point and to the columns
the blob occupies, and only where they currently belong to the band being moved from.
Justification | Why the examination is limited
At most 60 bottom points are examined per component, and accepting one point suppresses the
columns within 0.35 pitches of it. Both are cost controls. A long word has hundreds of columns
and the upward walk at each is not free, while the suppression prevents the same ring being found
again from every column it spans. The cap is a deliberate compromise: a word with more than 60
distinct bottom points may have a ring missed, which costs one misplaced dot, whereas examining
every column adds work; no per-page timing effect is established here.

neighbouring line’s x-height band, within 0.2 pitches of its centre, and if so to move it there.

The ownership array as it stood before the two dot corrections is passed in so that the pixels they
moved can be identified, by comparing the two arrays. A small compact fragment that sits on pixels

by the dot rule has no ink in its line’s x-height band, by the very nature of being a dot, so it looks

them as they are found would mean later tests read ownership that earlier moves had already
changed, so the outcome would depend on the order the bands happened to be visited. Collecting
first and applying afterwards makes the result independent of that order.

This function contains no logic of its own. It runs the band guess and then the three corrections, in

Justification | Why the rules are separate functions
The initial ownership follows the seam bands; subsequent corrections are project-specific rules for
candidate fragments and connections. Separate helpers make those conditions inspectable. Historical
ablation claims require the corresponding run records; the existence of a helper does not establish
how its contribution was measured.
Justification | Why the order is fixed
The sequence is not arbitrary. The band guess must come first because everything else corrects it.
The two welding rules come next, and they are the most specific: each requires several independent
conditions and fires rarely. The fragment rule comes last and is the most general, which is the right
place for it, because a general rule run first would act on cases the specific rules would have handled
better. The ordering principle, specific before general, is the same one that governs a cascade of
fallbacks in LinePitch: apply the best-informed rule wherever it applies, and the broad rule only to
what is left.
The dependency between them is explicit in the arguments. The fragment rule receives the ownership
array as it stood before the welding rules ran, precisely so it can recognise and respect their decisions.
That is why the band guess returns that copy, rather than each rule working from whatever it finds.

Method | Building the alpha channel
The crop must show this line’s ink and not the neighbouring lines’ intrusions, so a per-pixel weight is
needed saying how much of each pixel to show. That weight is calledalpha, borrowing the standard
graphics term for opacity, where 1 means fully shown and 0 fully replaced by white.
It starts as the ownership mask for this line, enlarged to the crop size bilinearly. Bilinear rather
than nearest-neighbour is a deliberate choice here, and for an unusual reason: the soft edge that
interpolation produces is what makes the stroke boundary in the final crop look like a real pen edge
rather than a staircase of hard pixels. The slight blur is the feature, not an artefact to be tolerated.
Method | Recovering ink the mask missed
The half-size mask inevitably misses some faint ink, and at full resolution that ink is visible. So a
second, local threshold is computed, on the crop alone rather than the whole page, using the same
divide-by-local-background method as InkMask but with a radius scaled to the crop’s own height.
Because the crop is one line of writing rather than a whole page, the contrast within it is far more
uniform, so this local threshold can pick up strokes that the page-wide one could not.
Those recovered pixels cannot simply be added, or the neighbouring lines’ ink would come back with
them. Two gates restrict them.

that neighbourhood. The reasoning is that a stroke the mask missed lies next to strokes it
caught, since it is part of the same writing, whereas ink from the line above or below is further
away.
• The ownership veto.Any pixel the page-level ownership already gave to a different line is
excluded, unconditionally. This gate is enlarged with nearest-neighbour rather than bilinear
interpolation, precisely the opposite choice from the alpha channel, and for the opposite reason:
ownership is a yes-or-no fact about which line a pixel belongs to, and a blurred version would
half-assign a pixel to two lines at once.

recovery can only ever add ink and never remove it.

Method | Background: what a state dictionary is
Astate dictionaryis the standard way to store a trained network: a mapping from the name of
each parameter to its values. A name likestage1.0.weight encodes a position in the network, here
the weight array of layer 0 of the block called stage1. The network’s structure is not stored at all; it
is written in code, and loading consists of looking up the names that code expects. That is why the

script that wrote the file and the code that reads it.
Method | The .npz format
An .npz file is a zip archive of individual arrays, each stored under a name. That suits a state
dictionary exactly, and it needs no library beyond numpy, which is the constraint this project works
under.
Justification | Why pickling is refused
The file is opened with object pickling disabled.Picklingis a mechanism for storing arbitrary Python
objects, and restoring one executes code from the file, so a checkpoint able to contain pickled objects
is able to run anything when loaded. Refusing it restricts the file to plain numeric arrays, which is all
a set of weights needs to be. It also acts as a check on the files themselves: a checkpoint that will not
load without pickling is storing something other than arrays, and that is worth discovering rather
than tolerating.
Method | Keys beginning with a double underscore
Names starting with a double underscore are skipped when building the parameter dictionary, because
they hold metadata rather than weights. One is read specially: a list of writer names, which is
converted into a mapping from each name to its output slot.
Carrying that mapping inside the checkpoint matters more than it appears. The namer outputs
one score per slot, and a slot means nothing without knowing which writer it stands for. If the
correspondence were kept separately, in a configuration file or in code, then a checkpoint trained on a
different set of writers, or on the same writers in a different order, would load without complaint and
attribute every page to the wrong person. Storing the names with the weights makes that mismatch
impossible.

+1 puts the input on the scale the initialisation assumed.

The array is given the shape (1, 1, height, width) to match the four-axis convention described in the
chapter introduction: one image in the batch, one channel in that image. The axes are necessary even
though both lengths are 1, because every layer indexes by position and would otherwise misinterpret
which axis is which.

of what the training code did. A network is only correct on inputs prepared the way its training

Purpose | The problem it solves
A network asked to identify a writer from a raw crop will use whatever is most reliably distinctive, and

patch, which matches the fact that a stroke, a corner or a loop is a local arrangement of ink. And it

without changing it: the same filter detects a vertical stroke wherever on the line it occurs. A plain
fully connected layer has neither property; it would have to learn what a vertical stroke looks like
separately at every position, needing enormously more parameters and far more examples.

the loops.
Method | The strided view and reshape storage
The patches are not assembled by copying. Neighbouring patches overlap heavily, a 3 by 3 filter at
stride 1 sharing six of nine pixels with its neighbour, so a literal im2col would duplicate most of
the input nine times over. Instead the columns are produced as astrided view, which needs some
explanation.
A numpy array is a flat block of memory plus a set ofstrides, one per axis, each saying how many
bytes to step to advance by one along that axis. Indexing is then just arithmetic on those strides.
109

Handwriting Robot Code theory DemoCode edition
Supplying a different shape and a different set of strides therefore produces an array that reads the
same memory in a different pattern, as a view without an initial patch copy; a later reshape can
still materialise storage. Here a six-axis view is constructed whose axes are batch, channel, filter
row, filter column, output row and output column, so that the patches appear laid out ready to be
reshaped into columns. The strides for the two output axes are the input’s own row and column
strides multiplied by the stride, which is what makes stepping to the next output position step the
right distance through the image.
A strided view of overlapping patches reports a shape far larger than the memory behind it, because
the same bytes appear at many positions. That is safe to read and would be meaningless to write
to. The reshape that follows does force one copy, since the pattern cannot be expressed as strides
alone, but it is one copy instead of nine.
Method | The bias
One learned number per output channel is added to every position of that channel. It lets a filter shift
its whole response up or down, which matters because the squashing that follows treats zero specially:
without a bias, a filter could only ever decide between zero and its raw response, whereas with one
it can set the level at which it starts responding at all. Adding one number to a whole channel is
written as a reshape to four axes and a plain addition, relying onbroadcasting, numpy’s rule that
an axis of length 1 is repeated as needed to match the other operand.

110

Handwriting Robot Code theory DemoCode edition
Justification | Why that particular order
The order is not arbitrary and each adjacency has a reason. Normalisation comes after the convolution
because its purpose is to fix the scale of the convolution’s output, which it cannot do before that
output exists. ReLU comes after normalisation because the normalisation needs to see the signed
values to standardise them meaningfully; applied to an already rectified signal, with its mass piled at
zero, the mean and variance would describe mostly how many units were silent. And ReLU must
come before the next convolution, since the whole point of an activation is to break the chain of linear
operations.
A further consequence of this order is that the convolution’s bias is redundant: the normalisation
immediately subtracts a mean, which removes any constant the bias added. It is kept because the
checkpoint stores it and the trained values must be applied as they were learned, but it is worth
knowing that it has no effect on the result.
Method | How a layer is located in the checkpoint
Within a block the layers are numbered in threes, so group i occupies positions 3i for the convolution
and 3i+1 for the normalisation, the activation having no parameters and so no position of its own.
The names are built by joining the prefix and those numbers, which is how a checkpoint saved by
the training framework names its layers. The pattern is effectively a contract, and the next entry
describes what happens when it is relied on across different files.
Justification | The three stages, and why they get deeper
• stage1, two groups,on the full-resolution crop, where a filter sees a 3 by 3 patch of actual
pixels and so can only detect the smallest features: an edge, a stroke, the direction of a line.
• stage2, four groups,after one pooling, where features combine into corners, junctions and
curves.
• stage3, six groups,after a second pooling, where a filter’s receptive field covers a large part
of a letter and the features become letter-like.
The number of groups increases with depth because the number of distinguishable patterns does.
There are few ways to arrange ink in a 3 by 3 patch and a great many ways to arrange strokes into a
letter, so the later stages need more capacity. Placing the deepest stage after two poolings is also
what makes this affordable: it runs on a sixteenth of the original area, so its six groups cost less than
stage1’s two.

the next layer with a known mean and spread.

in the same units as the values themselves. Tostandardiseis to subtract the mean and divide by
the standard deviation, which leaves a quantity with mean 0 and standard deviation 1 regardless of

Justification | The reason for this construction

PyTorch supplies Linear, ReLU, Sigmoid and related layers. NumPy already executes elementwise

an exponential for the alternatives.

After a convolution, a positive value means the filter’s pattern was found and a negative one means
something like its opposite was. ReLU discards the negatives entirely, which is to say the layer reports
where each featurewaspresent and stays silent about where it was not. The next layer therefore
builds on evidence of presence rather than on a signed score, which is the behaviour that makes
stacked filters compose into detectors for larger shapes: strokes into corners, corners into loops, loops
into letters.

After ReLU, a value is evidence that a feature is present, and zero is silence. The maximum answers
"was this feature found anywhere in this window", which is the useful question about evidence. An
average would dilute a strong local response by the surrounding silence, so a thin stroke correctly

place, and this file uses it later where the question genuinely is about a typical level rather than a
presence.
Method | Implementation, and the discarded remainder
The windows are formed as a strided view, by the same mechanism described under Conv2d, with
two extra axes for position within the window; taking the maximum over those two axes then pools
everything at once. An odd final row or column, which cannot fill a window, is dropped before the
view is built. Discarding input is acceptable here because the loss is a single row or column at the
edge of a padded crop, where there is no ink, while the alternative of padding would introduce a
window containing invented values whose maximum could be reported as a detected feature.

be high. This is a property of the output layer, not a fault in the training, and any use of the
namer on an unknown writer has to account for it.

Purpose | The problem: a column is not enough
After the convolutional backbone the line has become a sequence of feature vectors, one per column.
Classifying each column on its own would be hopeless. A single narrow column of a handwritten line
is often ambiguous even to a person: the left half of an a and the left half of a d are the same stroke,
and which it is depends on what follows. A smudge is identifiable only from the letters around it.
What is needed is a layer whose output at each column depends on the whole line, and that is what a
recurrentlayer provides.
Method | Background: what recurrence means
Arecurrent neural networkprocesses a sequence one step at a time, carrying a vector of numbers
from each step to the next. That carried vector is thehidden state, and it is the network’s summary
of everything seen so far. At each step the layer combines the new input with the incoming hidden
state to produce a new hidden state, which is also its output for that step. The same weights are
used at every step, so the layer has a fixed number of parameters however long the sequence is.
Justification | Why a plain recurrent layer is not used
In a plain recurrent layer the hidden state is overwritten at every step, as a weighted combination of
the old state and the new input passed through a squashing function. Information therefore survives
only by being repeatedly multiplied by the recurrent weights. Over a hundred and sixty steps that
product either shrinks to nothing or grows without bound, depending on whether the weights are on
average below or above the scale that preserves magnitude. These are thevanishingandexploding
gradientproblems, and the practical consequence is that a plain recurrent layer cannot learn to
connect events more than a few steps apart. For reading a line of writing that is useless, since the
evidence resolving an ambiguous letter can be a whole word away.
Alternatives | The LSTM idea: a cell you add to rather than overwrite
Thelong short-term memorylayer [40] solves this by keeping a second vector, thecell state,
whose default behaviour is to persist unchanged. It is not recomputed each step; it is modified, by
having some of its contents erased and some new contents added. Because the default is to carry
forward, information can survive arbitrarily many steps without being multiplied by anything, which
is precisely what the plain layer could not do.
What to erase, what to add and what to reveal are decided by threegates, each a vector of numbers
between 0 and 1 produced by a sigmoid. A gate value of 0 blocks completely, 1 lets everything through,
and anything between is a proportion. A fourth quantity, the candidate, supplies the contents that
might be added.

The cell update is the heart of the method and is worth reading slowly. It is an addition, not a
replacement. If the forget gate is 1 and the input gate is 0 at some position, that position of the
cell passes through completely untouched, for as many steps as those gate values persist. No weight
matrix is applied to it along the way, so it neither shrinks nor grows. That is the path along which
information travels a long distance, and it is what the name long short-term memory refers to: a
short-term memory that can be made to last.

Method | How all four gates are computed at once
The four weight matrices are stored stacked into one array, four times the hidden size tall. One matrix
multiplication therefore produces all four pre-activation vectors end to end, and the implementation
simply slices the result into four equal blocks in the order input, forget, candidate, output. That
ordering is not a choice made here; it is the convention of the framework the weights were trained
with, and slicing in a different order would silently use the forget gate’s weights as the input gate’s.
One large matrix multiplication is also considerably faster than four small ones, for the BLAS reasons
given under Conv2d.
Justification | Why there are two biases
Mathematically a single bias would do, since adding two constants is adding one constant. Both are
kept because the framework that trained the weights stores both, and the trained values must be
applied as they were learned. Their sum is what has any effect.
Justification | Why this loop cannot be vectorised
Every other layer in this file processes its whole input at once. This one cannot, and the reason is
structural rather than a shortcoming of the implementation: step t needs the hidden and cell state
from step t−1, so the steps are genuinely sequential. Within a step everything is already whole-array
arithmetic across the batch and the hidden positions. This is the same situation as the column loop
in LeastCostSeam, and the same conclusion holds: the loop is over the one axis that is irreducibly
ordered.
Both states start as vectors of zeros. Zero is the natural choice for "nothing seen yet", and it has
the useful property that an all-zero cell with a forget gate near 1 stays empty until something is
deliberately written into it.

Justification | Why one direction is not enough
An LSTM reading left to right has, at each column, seen everything to the left and nothing to the
right. For handwriting that is half the available evidence and often the less useful half. Consider the
stroke that begins both an a and a d: what distinguishes them is the ascender that comes afterwards.
A left-to-right reader at the start of that letter cannot know. It will often get the answer right in
the end, because the output at the later column can be correct, but its representation of the earlier
columns is impoverished, and the earlier columns are where CTC may want to place the character.
Method | The construction
The remedy is to run a second, completely separate LSTM over the sequence reversed, then put its
outputs back into forward order and join the two side by side. Each position then carries a summary
of everything to its left, from the forward pass, and a summary of everything to its right, from the
backward pass. The two have independent weights throughout; nothing is shared.

Reading the future is only possible because the whole line is available before any output is needed. A
system transcribing speech as it is spoken could not do this, since the future has not happened yet.

at once. Bidirectional recurrence is standard in handwriting recognition for exactly this reason, and
the architecture this network follows is built on it [35].

costs nothing extra in memory. The output of the backward pass is reversed again so that position
t of both halves refers to the same column; forgetting that second reversal would align each position
with its mirror image and produce fluent-looking nonsense.

symmetric, since every edit has an inverse of the same cost, so swapping cannot change the answer,
and it makes the retained row as short as possible.

followed that order.

Slant comes from a shear search that concentrates ink into columns. Ascender and descender extents,
advances, lead spacing and word gaps are measured in x-height units; robust summaries reduce
isolated extraction errors. These features are explicit geometric measurements, unlike learned CNN
features. Their meaning still depends on body-band and alignment quality.

Two conditions together. It is short, under 2.5 pixels of path length. And it isdangling, meaning at
least one of its two endpoints is not shared with any other path, so it leads nowhere. Requiring both
is what makes the test safe: a short path joined at both ends is a genuine short connection between
two strokes and must be kept, while a long dangling path is a real stroke with a free end, such as the
stem of a t.
The sharing is determined by counting how many paths have an endpoint at each coordinate. A count
of one means that endpoint belongs to this path alone.
Justification | Why the threshold is in pixels and not x-heights
Almost every threshold in this file is in x-heights, for the scale-independence reasons given in the
introduction. This one is deliberately not, because the artefact it targets is not a property of the
writing at all: it is a property of the thinning algorithm, whose spurs are a few pixels long whatever
the resolution, because thinning works pixel by pixel. A threshold in x-heights would grow with
resolution and start removing real strokes from high-resolution crops.
If the pruning would remove everything, the original paths are returned instead. A glyph consisting
entirely of short dangling paths is most likely debris, but returning nothing would hide it from the
filters that are designed to judge it; returning it unchanged lets them do so.

them separate misrepresents the writing: the glyph appears to have more strokes than it does, and a
plotter drawing it would lift the pen where the writer did not.

heading one way and another leaves heading the same way, they were one stroke. If the second leaves
at a sharp angle, the junction is a real corner or a crossing of two different strokes.

Justification | Why the dot product is negated
This is the step most easily got wrong. Both directions are measuredoutwardfrom their own path’s
end. Two paths that continue through a junction therefore point in opposite directions: one arrives
pointing into the junction, the other leaves pointing away, and as outward measurements those are
roughly antiparallel. So perfect continuation gives a dot product of−1, not +1, and negating it turns
continuation into a cosine of +1, which is what the angle formula expects.
Justification | Why the cosine is clipped
The inverse cosine is defined only on the range−1 to 1. Two unit vectors cannot mathematically
produce a dot product outside it, but floating-point rounding can: a vector whose length is stored as
1.0000000001 yields a dot product a fraction beyond 1, and the inverse cosine of that is not a number.
The result would then propagate silently through every comparison, since comparisons involving it
are all false. Clipping first costs nothing and removes the possibility.
Justification | Why 75 degrees is generous
A threshold of 75 degrees permits substantial direction change at a skeleton junction. The qualitative
trade-off is between leaving a plausible continuation split and joining branches that were separate.
Incorrect joining can alter stroke order, connections and shape, not merely the stroke count. The exact
75-degree value is a project heuristic; its optimality and asymmetric error costs are not established by
the algorithm citation.

Justification | Why it repeats until nothing changes
One merge can create a new opportunity. Three paths meeting in a line are joined by first merging
two, after which the merged path has a new free end that may continue into the third. So the search
repeats until a pass finds nothing to merge. Each pass also takes the single best candidate, the
pair with the smallest turn angle, rather than merging everything that qualifies. That matters at a
junction where three or more paths meet and more than one pairing is permissible: taking the best
first means the most convincing continuation is committed to before the others are considered, which
is the greedy strategy used for the line centres in segment.py, but this greedy order does not prove
globally correct reconstruction.
The search compares every pair of ends on every pass, which is quadratic in the number of paths
and runs inside a loop. That would matter for hundreds of paths; here it runs on the handful
belonging to one letter, where the cost is irrelevant and the clarity of an exhaustive search is worth
having.

Method | The Douglas-Peucker method
The algorithm [33] is recursive and rests on one idea: a path can be replaced by the straight line
between its endpoints if no point on it strays far from that line. So measure the furthest stray; if it
is within tolerance, the whole path becomes two points, and if not, the path is split at the furthest
point and each half is simplified the same way.

A loop, such as the body of an o, defeats the basic method. Its endpoints coincide or nearly so,
which makes the reference line a point rather than a line, and every distance measured from it is
meaningless. The function detects this by checking whether the far end of the path returns close to
the start, and if so splits the path first at the point furthest from the start, simplifying the two halves
separately. Each half is then an ordinary open path with distinct endpoints, and the method applies.
The two halves are rejoined by dropping the last point of the first before concatenating, since the
split point belongs to both and would otherwise be stored twice. A duplicated point is a zero-length
segment, which is harmless to draw but divides by zero in any calculation that normalises by
segment length.

Purpose | What it is for, and the idea behind it
Reproducing a hand is not only a matter of letter shapes. The output must alsolooklike a photograph
of handwriting to the networks that judge it, and that involves properties no glyph library captures:
how much of the image is ink, how dark the ink is, how bright the paper is, the proportions of the
line. This function measures those on a real line, so that synthesis has a target to match rather than
having to guess.
Method | Background: domain shift
Domain shiftis the name for the situation where a model is used on data drawn from a different
distribution than it was trained on. A network trained on photographs of handwriting has learned
163

Handwriting Robot Code theory DemoCode edition
the statistics of photographs: paper that is not pure white, ink that is not pure black, and soft grey
edges where the two meet. Rendering a synthetic line as pure black on pure white produces an image
that is correct as geometry but statistically unlike anything in training, and the network’s response to
it is unreliable, which would corrupt the judgement of the output.
This is why the paper and ink levels are measured as percentiles of the real crop rather than assumed:
the median of the bright pixels is what this writer’s paper actually is, and the median of the dark
pixels is what their ink actually is. The fraction of intermediate greys is measured too, since that
describes the softness of the stroke edges.
Justification | Why the word gap is measured from the ink, not the recogniser
The width of the space character as the aligner reports it is not a reliable measure of how widely
this writer spaces their words. CTC concentrates its output and tends to assign a space a narrow
territory, well inside the actual gap. So the gap is measured directly instead: the columns with no ink
are found, the runs between inked columns are collected, those under half an x-height are discarded
as being gaps within a word, and the median of the rest is taken.
The half-x-height threshold is what separates the two kinds of gap. Within a word the pen may lift,
leaving a small gap, but a word boundary is a deliberate space and is substantially wider. The median
of the wide gaps therefore describes word spacing, and the median again rather than the mean, so
that one unusually wide gap at a paragraph end does not inflate it.
Justification | Why slant, ascender and descender are measured here too
These are also measured in the profile from the glyphs themselves, so measuring them again on the
rendered line looks redundant. It is not, and the comment in the code gives the reason: these are
measuredthe same waythey will be measured on the synthesised output. A quantity measured by
two different methods is not comparable with itself, so to check whether the synthesis reproduced
the writer’s slant, both sides must be measured by the same procedure. These values exist to be the
reference half of that comparison.
Fields that cannot be measured are filled with a not-a-number value rather than a plausible default.
That is deliberate: the caller takes a median across lines with those values excluded, so a line
that could not be measured contributes nothing, whereas a default would contribute a fabricated
measurement that is indistinguishable from a real one.

At least three variants are kept whatever the proportion says, and the filter does nothing at all when

dropping below it costs more than the bad variant does. For a rare character, having three imperfect
examples is better than having one perfect one, because synthesis needs something to choose among

Purpose | The problem beyond resampling
Resampling makes two strokes have the same number of points, but corresponding points still need to
be at corresponding places, and two things can spoil that. A stroke may be traced in either direction,
so one writing of a letter may run left to right and another right to left, in which case point 0 of one
corresponds to point N−1 of the other. And a closed loop has no inherent starting point at all, so
two tracings of the same o may begin anywhere on the circle.
Method | The two fixes
• Open strokes are oriented left to right.If the stroke ends left of where it began, it is
reversed. Left to right is chosen because it is the direction of writing, so it is the orientation
most strokes already have.
• Closed strokes are rotated to begin at their leftmost point.A stroke is recognised as
closed when its two ends come within 0.3 x-heights of each other. The points are then rotated
so the leftmost becomes first, and the original start is appended to close the loop. The leftmost
point is used because it is well defined for any loop and is found identically in every tracing of it.
Both fixes work by choosing a canonical form: a rule that picks, from among the several equivalent
ways of representing the same stroke, one particular way that depends only on the shape. Any such
rule works provided every stroke obeys the same one, which is the real requirement.
Without these fixes the averaging would not merely be inaccurate; it would be nonsense. Averaging
a stroke with a reversed copy of itself yields a shape collapsing toward its own midpoint, since the
first point of one is averaged with the last of the other. The prototype would be a smear through
the middle of the letter.

Every individual variant carries noise: the staircase left by the pixel grid, a boundary placed a little

Only variants with the same number of strokes can be averaged, because the averaging matches
strokes one to one. The variants are grouped by stroke count and the largest group is used. Taking
the largest rather than any particular count lets the data decide how the writer usually forms the
letter: if most of their a’s are one stroke, the prototype is a one-stroke a.

is the least from which an average means anything. The five-stroke limit guards against averaging
glyphs whose stroke counts are high because the tracing fragmented them, where the stroke-to-stroke
matching would be matching pieces that do not correspond.

Within the group, each variant’s strokes are sorted by their leftmost point and matched by position
in that order, then aligned and resampled to a common 44 points. Sorting by position is a weak way

person occur in a consistent left-to-right arrangement, so the leftmost stroke of one a is the same
stroke as the leftmost of another.

and they define the glyph’s extent. Smoothing them would pull them inward, shortening every stroke
slightly with each pass and, worse, moving the attachment points that synthesis relies on.

def Apply(writer, drop=None, keep=None, curated=False, outName=None):
prof, path = LoadProfile(writer, curated)
glyphs = dict(prof.get("glyphs") or {})
drop = {k: set(v) for k, v in (drop or {}).items() if v}
keep = {k: set(v) for k, v in (keep or {}).items()}
for ch in list(drop)+list(keep):
if ch not in glyphs:
raise SystemExit("%r has no variants in %s" % (ch, path.name))
removed, emptied = 0, []
for ch, vs in list(glyphs.items()):
if ch in keep:
chosen = [g for i, g in enumerate(vs) if i in keep[ch]]
elif ch in drop:
chosen = [g for i, g in enumerate(vs) if i not in drop[ch]]
else:
continue
removed += len(vs)-len(chosen)
if not chosen:
emptied.append(ch)
del glyphs[ch]
else:
glyphs[ch] = chosen
prof["glyphs"] = glyphs
ideal = dict(prof.get("idealGlyphs") or {})
medoid = dict(prof.get("idealMedoid") or {})
adv = dict(prof.get("letterAdvance") or {})
touched = set(drop) | set(keep)
for ch in touched:
if ch not in glyphs:
ideal.pop(ch, None)
medoid.pop(ch, None)
adv.pop(ch, None)
continue
vs = glyphs[ch]
p = Prototype(ch, vs)
m = Medoid(ch, vs)
if p is None:
ideal.pop(ch, None)
else:
ideal[ch] = p
if m is None:
medoid.pop(ch, None)
else:
medoid[ch] = m
adv[ch] = round(float(np.median([g["advance"] for g in vs])), 3)
prof["idealGlyphs"] = ideal
prof["idealMedoid"] = medoid
prof["letterAdvance"] = adv

def Medoid(ch, vs):
grids = [(ST._ShapeGrid(g), g) for g in vs]
grids = [(v, g) for v, g in grids if v is not None]
if len(grids) < 2:
return None
G = np.stack([v for v, _ in grids])
D = np.abs(G[:, None, :]-G[None, :, :]).sum(-1)
med = grids[int(np.argmin(D.sum(1)))][1]
return dict(strokes=[ST.SmoothStroke(s) for s in med["strokes"]],
priorD=round(float(med.get("priorD", 0.5)), 4),
advance=round(float(med.get("advance", 0.9)), 3),

width=round(float(med.get("width", 0.9)), 3),
top=round(float(med.get("top", 1.0)), 3),
bot=round(float(med.get("bot", 0.0)), 3),
entryY=round(float(med.get("entryY", 0.3)), 3),
exitY=round(float(med.get("exitY", 0.3)), 3),

def DrawGlyph(g, cell=150, pad=14):
from PIL import Image, ImageDraw
im = Image.new("L", (cell, cell), 255)
d = ImageDraw.Draw(im)
strokes = g.get("strokes") or []
pts = [p for s in strokes for p in s]
if not pts:
return im
xs = [p[0] for p in pts]
ys = [p[1] for p in pts]
w = max(1e-6, max(xs)-min(xs))
h = max(1e-6, max(ys)-min(ys))
k = (cell-2*pad)/max(w, h)
ox = (cell-w*k)/2.0
oy = (cell-h*k)/2.0
for s in strokes:
q = [(ox+(p[0]-min(xs))*k, cell-(oy+(p[1]-min(ys))*k)) for p in s]
if len(q) > 1:
d.line(q, fill=0, width=2)
return im

study or proof that the threshold transfers to new writers. Rebuilding profiles with different extraction
can change the measurement even if the nominal formula is unchanged.

9.1.6 Full candidate and repair algorithm, with limitations
Generate at least one candidate, using seeds+977k for trialk; render at controlled ink width; recognise
its text; obtain writer probability; computeJ; retain the strictly better complete candidate. Stop at
the trial budget or the configured near-perfect score. The integer 977 spaces seeds deterministically.
Being prime does not prove statistically independent draws. The direct joint function defaults use six
tries, three repair rounds and two new weak positions per round, with early thresholds 0.99 and 0.995.
These are search-cost limits and stopping preferences, not character-accuracy targets guaranteed on
paper.

complete trajectory and rescores it. Commit the new anchor assignments only if the complete joint
score improves. The result’s best score is then nondecreasing for deterministic scoring, but there is
no global-optimum guarantee: regenerated geometry, wrapping and writer cues interact. A failed
local change does not prove that character cannot be improved by another choice. The removed older
legibility-only routine had different defaults and acceptance bookkeeping; it must not be described as
the joint algorithm merely because names are similar.

wrong l, so the floor keeps at least a third of the designed reach whatever the measurement says.

Justification | Why the pen-up moves are implicit
Nothing records the lifts explicitly. They are implied by the boundaries between strokes, because by
definition the pen must rise at the end of one and fall at the start of the next. Storing them would
duplicate information already present and create the possibility of the two disagreeing, which is a
class of bug that cannot arise if the state is stored once.
Method | The coordinate convention, and the one place it changes
Coordinates are millimetres with y increasing upward, which is the natural orientation for describing
writing and the convention the stored glyphs use. Images have y increasing downward, and some
machines expect one or the other. Rather than taking a position on that, the trajectory states its own
convention and each consumer converts: the rasteriser flips y as it draws, and the G-code writer flips
it if the machine needs it. The flip therefore happens at the boundary, once per consumer, rather
than being half-applied inside the trajectory.

quantity a stroke-ordering optimisation would try to reduce.

derived measurements of that same data, which is what a class is for. The rest of the pipeline is
plain functions, because elsewhere there is no state that several operations need to share.

This maps the prior distance onto a 0 to 1 scale between the two reference points, which is what lets
a single expression cover the whole middle range. The swap probability is then lam times a factor
running from 0.55 at the clean end to 1.45 at the garbage end, clipped to 1. So at a given lam, a
worse shape is swapped more often, and at a given quality, a less trusted library is swapped more
often. The two inputs act multiplicatively, which is the behaviour wanted: neither alone should force
a swap.
Justification | Why a probability and not a decision
Returning a probability rather than a yes or no is what produces a mixed page, and a mixed page is
the point. A threshold rule would draw every instance of a given character from the same source, so a
letter whose shape sits near the line would be either always the writer’s or always the anchor. With
a probability, some instances are theirs and some are not, which both preserves more of the hand
and spreads the risk: one bad instance of a letter in a line is recoverable from context, where every
instance being bad is not.
Because the draw is made per glyph from a seeded generator, the same text and seed give the same
page. That is what makes the best-of-N search meaningful, since each attempt differs only by its
seed, and what makes a result reproducible rather than something that happened once.

Justification | Why this works, and what it is really measuring
The chain of reasoning behind it is the substantive part. The prior distance measures how far a
stored shape sits from what its letter should look like. A library whose shapes sit far from that is a
library of bad cuts. Bad cuts come from boundaries placed where no honest boundary exists. And
that happens exactly when the writing is joined up, because in cursive the pen does not lift between
letters, so there is no place to cut that does not damage something.
So the median prior distance is, indirectly, a measure of how cursive the hand is, arrived at by
measuring the consequence rather than the cause. That is why it works as a trust signal: it responds
to the thing that actually makes an extraction unreliable. And it is why heavily cursive writers end
up drawn from anchor forms, which is the mechanism behind this project’s finding that such hands
reproduce less faithfully.
Justification | Why an empty library returns 1
With no variants there is nothing to measure and nothing to draw from, so the anchor is the only
available source and lam 1 states that. Returning 0 instead would claim a library worth trusting, and
the caller would then try to draw from one that does not exist.
A profile may carry an explicit legibilityLambda, which callers prefer over this function. That is
how a value found by experiment for a particular writer can override the derived one, and it is why
the stored lam column appears in this project’s profile tables even though it is usually empty.

as a tiny one. Real variation behaves the first way: most letters are close to the writer’s usual form
and a few are noticeably off. A uniform draw produces output that wobbles unconvincingly, because
every letter is about equally displaced.

The vertical amplitude is 0.6 of the horizontal. Vertical position is read more sharply than horizontal:
the eye uses the baseline as a reference, so a letter sitting high stands out in a way that one sitting
slightly right does not. The recogniser is similarly sensitive, since its features were learned relative to
the baseline. Reducing the vertical component keeps the variation from reading as a fault.

anchor glyph, by CORE_JITTER_FRAC. So the same function serves for a fully varied extracted
glyph and a nearly rigid anchor, with the policy decision kept in the caller rather than here.

gives a path whose density varies several-fold along its length, and two later stages are sensitive to
that.
• The rasteriseruses distances to complete line segments in DrawPolyline, so sparse vertices do
not inherently create dotted straight segments; resampling changes the represented geometry
and amount of segment work.
• The G-code writeremits moves between points; point density affects command count and
curve approximation. Actual speed also depends on pulse timing and mechanics, so even spacing
does not establish constant physical pen speed.
Justification | Why 0.35 millimetres
The 0.35 mm sampling step controls trajectory point density. Finer spacing increases point storage
and later processing; coarser spacing gives fewer samples and can underrepresent curved geometry.
Segment-based drawing and motion interpolation also matter, so uniform samples alone do not
guarantee continuous raster coverage, smoother physical motion or constant actual pen speed. This
exact step is a project setting, not a literature optimum.
This duplicates _ResampleN in style.py, differing in that it takes a spacing rather than a count
and returns tuples rather than an array. Both forms are needed: averaging requires a fixed count
so that points correspond between strokes, while drawing requires a fixed spacing so that density is
uniform. The two interfaces serve different callers; count and spacing can be related through total
path length, subject to endpoint and rounding conventions.

because an explicit break is the writer’s instruction and must be obeyed wherever the line happens to
be, while a space is merely a place where a break is permitted. Keeping the two distinct lets layout
handle them as what they are.

and a trailing marker is removed so text ending in a newline does not produce an empty final line.
Both are small conveniences that keep the layout loop from needing to test for them.

a word occasionally overruns the requested line width by a small margin. That is the right direction
for the error to fall: a line a few percent too long is unremarkable, where a conservative estimate that
broke lines early would leave visible ragged gaps.

All the strokes are drawn and then the whole image is blurred once. Blurring each stroke as it was
drawn would be both slower and wrong: where two strokes overlap, each having been individually
softened, the overlap would be darker than a single stroke’s core, producing a visible dark patch at
every crossing. Blurring the finished image treats a crossing as the single region of ink that it is.
The canvas is sized from the trajectory’s own bounds plus the margin, so it is exactly as large as
the writing requires. A fixed canvas size would either clip long text or surround short text with
blank paper, and the second matters as much as the first, because the proportion of the crop that is
ink is one of the statistics the networks respond to.

def PageStrokes(gray, timer=None):
lines, _dbg, info = SEG.SegmentLines(gray, timer=timer)
strokes = []
perLine = []
for ln in lines:
crop = np.asarray(ln["image"], dtype=np.uint8)
ink = SEG.BinarizeLine(crop)
if not ink.any():
perLine.append(0)
continue
polys = ST.TracePolylines(SEG.Skeletonize(ink))
x0, y0 = (ln["bbox"][0], ln["bbox"][1]) if "bbox" in ln else (0, 0)
kept = 0
for p in polys:
if len(p) < MIN_STROKE_PTS:
continue
strokes.append([(float(x)+x0, -(float(y)+y0)) for (x, y) in p])
kept += 1
perLine.append(kept)
return strokes, dict(lines=len(lines), strokesPerLine=perLine, **info)

11.1.6 Pen state machine, dwell, overrun and debounce
The pen motor turns one way and the cam alternates states. The conceptual state machine is:
check interlocks; read current state; if already at target, do nothing; otherwise energise; poll until
target or timeout; optionally continue the pen-up seating overrun; de-energise; report success/failure.
The inspected SetPen compares feedback with the requested target, not always “up” as one report
pseudocode line suggests. A switch reporting not-up does not measure nib contact force. The
mechanism can satisfy a binary switch while pen pressure remains unsuitable.
The 40 ms up-overrun, 2 ms polling sleep, 3 s timeout and 350 ms G-code settling dwell serve different
roles. The report attributes dwell to visual tuning; it supplies no formal optimum for each. At an
illustrative unloaded 150 RPM, a quarter-turn takes 0.1 s, but gearing load, cam contact and switch
position make this unsuitable as a measured timing prediction. The same 350 ms dwell need not
represent the same physical settling process for raising and lowering.
Endstop confirmation requires three high reads, two gaps of 6 ms, hence 12 ms from first to last
sample. Under an unrealistic independent spurious high probabilityq, three samples would give
q3. Real contact bounce is time-correlated, so this is not a reliability estimate. Debounce rejects
short chatter at a cost of latency; it cannot ensure switches are “never” triggered by noise. The pen
feedback routine is distinct from the debounced endstop routine. At nominal 7.8125 mm/s, 12 ms
corresponds to 0.09375 mm of travelif motion continued; the inspected polling can pause pulses
during confirmation, so that multiplication is not a measured stopping distance.

Purpose | What it is for
A path may carry far more points than the machine can act on. A traced stroke has a point per pixel,
and resampling during layout placed points every 0.35 mm. This removes the points that are closer
together than the machine can resolve.
Justification | The method, and why it is not Douglas-Peucker
Each point is kept only if it is at least the minimum distance from the last point kept. This is a
different rule from the path simplification in style.py, which keeps points according to how far they
237

Handwriting Robot Code theory DemoCode edition
stray from a straight line, and the difference is appropriate to the different purpose. Here the question
is not whether a point carries shape information but whether the machine can act on it at all: a
commanded move shorter than the minimum segment is below the resolution of the motion, so it
costs a line in the file and produces nothing.
Justification | Why the comparison is against the last kept point
Comparing against the last kept point rather than the previous input point is what makes the rule
accumulate correctly. Against the previous input point, a long run of points each slightly under the
threshold would all be dropped, however far the path travelled in total. Against the last kept point,
the distance accumulates until the threshold is reached, so a point is emitted every minimum segment
along the path regardless of how finely the input was sampled.
The first and last points are always kept, whatever the spacing. The endpoints define where a stroke
begins and ends, so dropping one would shorten the stroke, and the final point in particular is
where the pen lifts and where the next stroke’s travel is measured from.

Purpose | What it is for
The strokes may be drawn in any order, since each is independent. The order determines how far the

a page of handwriting with hundreds of strokes the difference between a good order and a poor one is
substantial.
Purpose | Background: this is a travelling salesman problem
Finding the order that minimises total travel is thetravelling salesman problem: given a set of
places, find the shortest route visiting all of them. It is one of the classic hard problems in computing,
with no known method that finds the exact best route in reasonable time as the number of places
grows. With several hundred strokes an exact answer is out of reach, so aheuristicis used: a rule
that gives a good answer quickly with no guarantee of being best.
238

Handwriting Robot Code theory DemoCode edition
Method | The heuristic: bands, then nearest neighbour
Two ideas are combined. The strokes are first grouped into horizontal bands by their vertical centres,
and the bands are processed from top to bottom. Within a band, the nearest unvisited stroke is taken
next.
• Bandingexploits the structure of the problem. Text is arranged in lines, and almost all the
strokes of one line of writing are near each other, so a route that finishes one line before starting
the next is close to optimal. A pure nearest-neighbour search without banding can wander
between lines, since a stroke on the line below may happen to be nearer than the next stroke
along.
• Nearest neighbourwithin a band is the standard simple heuristic: from where the pen is, go
to the closest place not yet visited. It is greedy, so it can paint itself into a corner and leave a
long move to the last stroke, but within one line of text the strokes are nearly collinear and the
greedy route is close to the best.
