Method | Reversing a stroke to enter from the nearer end
A stroke can be drawn from either end, and the result is identical ink. So when the far end is closer
to the pen than the near end, the stroke is reversed. The code comment notes that this is free for
a plotter, and it is worth saying why: unlike a milling cut or an extrusion, a pen stroke has no
direction-dependent behaviour, so nothing is lost. It can nearly halve the travel to a long stroke.
Fewer than three strokes are returned unchanged. With two strokes there is only one meaningful
order, and the banding statistics would be computed from a sample too small to describe anything.

Justification | Why it exists when ToMachine already fits the drawing
The fitting scales the drawing to the available area, so in principle nothing can lie outside it. This
clamp exists for the cases where that reasoning does not hold: the fitting can be switched off by the
caller, the origin can be set such that the available area is computed wrongly, and a stroke can be
reversed or reordered by code that has no knowledge of the bounds. A point outside the work area is
not a cosmetic problem; it commands the machine to drive into its own frame.
Justification | Why the count is returned
Clamping silently would hide a real fault. A drawing that needed clamping was mispositioned, and
the clamped version is not what was asked for: the affected strokes are flattened against the boundary,
which is visible as a straight edge where writing should be. Returning the count lets the writer emit a
warning into the file, so the condition is recorded where someone will see it rather than inferred from
the drawing.
Clamping each coordinate independently is not geometrically principled: a stroke crossing the
boundary diagonally is bent rather than cut, so its shape changes. Properly clipping the path to the
rectangle would preserve the shape of the part inside. That is not done because the condition is a
fault to be reported rather than a case to be handled well, and the simple form cannot itself fail.

Justification | Why the machine clamps as well as the writer
The G-code writer already clamps to the configured bounds. This clamps again, against themeasured
usable area, and the two are not the same check. The writer’s bounds are configuration, stated in
advance; this one is what calibration actually found, which may be smaller, and it applies to any file
whatever its origin, including a hand-written one or one from another program.
The principle is that the machine must protect itself rather than trusting its input. A clamp at
the point of motion is the last line of defence and the only one that cannot be bypassed by using a
different generator.
Justification | Why it prints when it acts
A clamp that fires means the file asked for something outside the machine, so the drawing will be
wrong: strokes are flattened against the boundary. Printing the original and clamped coordinates
makes that visible while the job runs, so the operator can stop it rather than discovering afterwards
that part of the drawing is a straight line along one edge.

Justification | Why it watches the other switches
Each step checks for any switch other than the one being escaped and the ones explicitly ignored, and
stops if one trips. The code comment calls that a real fault, and it is: moving away from one limit
should not approach another, so if it does, the machine’s geometry is not what is believed, perhaps
because a switch is stuck closed or an axis is shorter than its recorded travel. Continuing to drive
would push against a second limit.
Justification | Why the position count is updated
The retract moves the carriage, so the recorded position must follow, or every subsequent absolute
move is out by the retract distance. The count is accumulated during the loop and applied to the
right axis afterwards, which also means a retract cut short by another switch updates by the distance
actually travelled rather than the distance intended.
Retracting at homing speed rather than drawing speed is deliberate. The machine is at a limit, in
a state it was not supposed to reach, and the geometry is not trusted. Moving slowly means the
other-switch check has time to act before much further travel occurs.

Purpose | What it is for
Drives one axis in one direction until a switch stops it, counting the steps. It is the primitive
the homing and calibration are built from, and the step count it returns is the measurement that
calibration converts into steps per millimetre.
Justification | Why the stopping condition is a test rather than a name
The caller supplies a function saying which switch is the expected one, rather than naming it. That is
necessary because homing begins without knowing which end of the axis it will reach: the carriage
may be anywhere, so driving in one direction may bring it to either switch. The first call accepts
either, and the second accepts only the opposite one.
Justification | Why an unexpected switch is an error rather than a stop
A switch that trips which is not the expected one raises an error naming the wiring, rather than being
treated as a normal stop. The distinction matters because the step count is about to be used as a
measurement: stopping on the wrong switch means the count does not measure what it is believed to,
and a calibration built on it would scale every subsequent move wrongly. A measurement known to
be invalid should fail rather than be used.
Justification | Why the step limit is also an error
Exceeding the step bound raises an error too. A correctly functioning machine reaches a switch in
a fraction of that distance, so the bound being reached means no switch is going to trip, which is
the disconnected-wiring case. Again the appropriate response is to stop and say so, since there is no
sensible way to proceed without a reference position.

Method | The measurement
The axis is driven in one direction until either switch trips, then reversed until the opposite one does,
counting the steps of the second move. That count is the full travel of the axis in steps, which divided
by the known travel in millimetres gives the steps per millimetre.
Justification | Why the count comes from the second move
The first move starts from wherever the carriage happened to be and ends at a switch, so its length is
arbitrary and carries no information. The second starts at a known position, one switch, and ends at
another known position, the other switch, so its length is the distance between two physical references.
Only a move between two known points measures anything.
Justification | Why the first switch is ignored during the reverse
The reverse move begins with the first switch still pressed, since the carriage is resting against it, and
it stays pressed for the first few steps until the lever releases. The code comment calls this release lag
and notes it is not a fault. Without adding that switch to the ignore set, the reverse move would
immediately detect it, decide it was unexpected, and raise an error on every calibration.
Justification | Why the other axis is ignored throughout
The other axis may be resting against one of its own limits while this one is being calibrated, which is
a perfectly normal state and nothing to do with this axis’s motion. Ignoring its switches lets each
axis be calibrated regardless of where the other happens to be parked.

Purpose | What this contributes

Inputs
cfgthe machine configuration
Output.a small mutable record holding whether the pen is up and how many pulses have been

Justification | Why the pen’s state must be tracked at all
This is the central peculiarity of the machine and it shapes the whole of the G-code writing. The pen
is raised and lowered by a geared motor that turns 90 degrees per pulse. It is aone-way actuator: it
accepts "move" and nothing else. There is no command meaning "be up", and nothing in the G-code
can ask where the pen currently is.
The consequence is that the writer must know the pen’s state by remembering it. The state begins at
a known value, assumed at power-on, and every pulse emitted flips it. Emitting a toggle when the pen
is already in the wanted state would move it to the wrong one, and from then on every pen command
in the file would be inverted: the machine would travel with the pen down and draw with it up.
Justification | Why it is a list rather than a plain value
The record is a two-element list so that the function updating it can modify it in place and the caller
sees the change. A tuple or an integer would be copied, and the caller would keep the old state. This
is the smallest possible piece of shared mutable state and it exists because the pen genuinely has a
state that persists across many lines of output.
The starting state is an assumption, not a measurement. If the machine is powered on with the pen
down, every pen command in the file is inverted. The hardware half resolves this properly, with a
switch that reports the pen’s actual position, but a written file cannot: it has no way to ask.

Purpose | What it is for
The safety check, called before essentially every step of every motion. It reads each switch and returns
the name of the first confirmed to be pressed.
Method | How the debounce is arranged
A switch reading open is dismissed immediately. One reading closed is then sampled twice more,
spaced by the debounce delay, and is believed only if all three agree. The reasoning behind the spacing
and the count is given under ENDSTOP_DEBOUNCE_S and ENDSTOP_CONFIRM_SAMPLES.
Justification | Why the asymmetry is what makes this affordable
This function runs before every step pulse, so its cost is multiplied by the tens of thousands of steps
in a drawing. The early dismissal is what keeps that cost down: in the normal case every switch
reads open and the function performs four pin reads and returns, with no delays at all. The twelve
milliseconds of confirmation are spent only when a switch actually reads closed, which happens once
per job at most.
Justification | Why some switches can be ignored
The ignore set exists because there are legitimate situations in which a switch is pressed and should
not stop the machine. Retracting off a switch necessarily begins with that switch pressed, and homing
one axis may hold a switch while the other axis is moved. Without the ability to disregard a named
switch, the only remedy would be to omit the safety check entirely during those operations, which
would remove it exactly where the machine is deliberately being driven against its limits.
The check returns at the first switch it confirms rather than examining all four. For stopping that
is sufficient, since one tripped switch is reason enough. The separate _AllTriggeredEndstops exists
for the emergency stop, which does need the full list so that it can retract off every one of them.

def SetPen(targetUp,timeoutS=3.0,force=False):
hit = TriggeredEndstop()
if hit is not None and not force:
print(f"Refusing pen move -- end-stop {hit} still tripped.")
return False
if PenIsUp()==targetUp:
return True
req.set_value(PEN_MOTOR_PIN,Value.ACTIVE)
deadline = time.time()+timeoutS
reached = False
while time.time()<deadline:
if not force and TriggeredEndstop() is not None:
break
if PenIsUp()==targetUp:
reached = True
break
time.sleep(0.002)
if reached and targetUp:
time.sleep(PEN_UP_OVERRUN_S)
req.set_value(PEN_MOTOR_PIN,Value.INACTIVE)
if not reached:
print("Pen move did NOT confirm via switch -- check motor/wiring.")
return reached

def BresenhamMove(dx,dy,stepDelayS=MIN_STEP_DELAY_S):
global CurrentXSteps,CurrentYSteps
ax,ay = abs(dx),abs(dy)
sx = 1 if dx>=0 else -1
sy = 1 if dy>=0 else -1
req.set_value(DIR1_PIN,AxisDirValue(INVERT_X,sx>0))
req.set_value(DIR2_PIN,AxisDirValue(INVERT_Y,sy>0))
def Pulse(stepPin):
req.set_value(stepPin,Value.ACTIVE)
time.sleep(stepDelayS)
req.set_value(stepPin,Value.INACTIVE)
if ax>=ay: #x is the major axis
err = ax//2
for _ in range(ax):
if abortEvent.is_set() or TriggeredEndstop() is not None:
return
Pulse(STEP1_PIN)
CurrentXSteps+=sx
err-=ay
if err<0: #the minor axis catches up by one step
Pulse(STEP2_PIN)
CurrentYSteps+=sy
err+=ax
else: #y is the major axis
err = ay//2

targetXMm,targetYMm = _ClampToUsableArea(targetXMm,targetYMm)
spmmX,spmmY = Calibration["steps_per_mm_x"],Calibration["steps_per_mm_y"]
x0Mm = CurrentXSteps/spmmX-EDGE_TOLERANCE_MM
y0Mm = CurrentYSteps/spmmY-EDGE_TOLERANCE_MM
distMm = math.hypot(targetXMm-x0Mm,targetYMm-y0Mm)

TargetYSteps = round((targetYMm+EDGE_TOLERANCE_MM)*spmmY)
dxSteps = TargetXSteps-CurrentXSteps
dySteps = TargetYSteps-CurrentYSteps

feedMmS = max(feedMmMin/60.0,GCODE_MIN_FEED_MM_S)

def _GcodeArcMove(x0Mm,y0Mm,x1Mm,y1Mm,iMm,jMm,clockwise,feedMmMin):
cx,cy = x0Mm+iMm,y0Mm+jMm
radius = math.hypot(iMm,jMm)
if radius<1e-6:
_GcodeLinearMove(x1Mm,y1Mm,feedMmMin)
return
startAngle = math.atan2(y0Mm-cy,x0Mm-cx)
endAngle = math.atan2(y1Mm-cy,x1Mm-cx)
if clockwise:
while endAngle>=startAngle: #force a strictly decreasing sweep
endAngle-=2.0*math.pi
else:
while endAngle<=startAngle:
endAngle+=2.0*math.pi
angleSpan = endAngle-startAngle
nSegments = max(4,int(abs(angleSpan)*radius/0.4)) #about 0.4 mm per chord
for k in range(1,nSegments+1):
if abortEvent.is_set() or TriggeredEndstop() is not None:
return
a = startAngle+angleSpan*(k/nSegments)
_GcodeLinearMove(cx+radius*math.cos(a),cy+radius*math.sin(a),feedMmMin)

An unguarded import of the hardware library would make this module unimportable off the machine,

Purpose | What this contributes
Connect abstract pen paths to modal movement and pen-state commands.
Output.an error type raised when an absolute move is attempted before homing.
Justification | Why calibration is a precondition and not a convenience
A stepper motor has no idea where it is. It moves a commanded number of steps from wherever it
happens to be, and nothing in the motor or the driver reports a position. So a command to move to
a particular place on the bed is meaningless until the machine has established where that place is
relative to its current position, which is what homing does.
Executing such a command anyway is not a silent error. The machine drives toward a position
computed from an unknown origin, which is as likely as not to be outside the bed, and it will drive
into its own frame until the limit switches catch it. A distinct error type refusing the command is the
appropriate response to a request that cannot be carried out safely.

Purpose | What this contributes
Connect abstract pen paths to modal movement and pen-state commands.
Output.nothing; it sets the outputs safe and releases the lines.
Method | The order of operations
The step pins and the pen motor are set inactive first, and only then are the lines released. The order
is necessary: once a line is released, its level is no longer controlled, and a line released while active
may stay active. Releasing a step pin while high would leave the driver holding a coil energised, which
heats the motor with nothing running to notice.
Justification | Why the release is in a finally clause
The setting of safe levels is wrapped so that the release happens whether or not it succeeded. If a pin
cannot be set, because the chip has gone away or the device was unplugged, the lines must still be
released, or they stay claimed by a process that has exited and the next run cannot acquire them.
Releasing a resource must not depend on the success of the tidying done before it.

the fault is cleared.
•Report,naming the switches and the retract distance.
Justification | Why re-entry is refused
The function returns immediately if the fault is already latched. Without that, a second switch
tripping during the retract would trigger another stop, which would retract again, which could trip
again, and the recursion would continue until the program ran out of stack. The guard makes the
stop happen once and the retract complete, which is the behaviour wanted: the first stop has already
established that the machine is to halt, and a second detection adds nothing.
Justification | Why the pen is raised
Raising the pen is part of stopping, not a courtesy. A pen left down during an abort rests on the paper
at the point of failure, where the ink bleeds into a visible blot, and if the machine is subsequently
moved by hand it drags a line across the drawing. The drawing is already spoiled by the abort; the
object is to avoid spoiling it further.

def ParseGcodeLine(raw)
Evidence | Source and method link
Software/DemoCode/reproduce.py line 803. Implementation evidence: [3]. Related method, alter-
natives and library discussion: Section 11.28.
Purpose | What this contributes
Connect abstract pen paths to modal movement and pen-state commands.
Inputs
rawone line of a G-code file
Output.the command and its parameters, or nothing for a line with no command.
Method | What it does
Strips comments, splits the line into words, takes the first G or M word as the command, and collects
the rest as parameters keyed by their letters.
Method | The two comment conventions
G-code has two: a semicolon makes the rest of the line a comment, and text in parentheses is a
comment wherever it appears, including in the middle of a line. Both are handled, the first by
truncating at the semicolon and the second by removing every parenthesised span. Handling only the
first would leave comment text to be parsed as words, and a comment containing a letter followed by
a digit would be read as a parameter.
Justification | Why the first G or M word becomes the command
A line has one command and any number of parameters, and the command is identified by being a G
or M word. Taking the first such word rather than the first word generally is what lets a line with a
leading line number be parsed, and the test that the command slot is still empty is what stops a later
G word being mistaken for a second command.
The command’s number is converted to an integer while parameters stay as floating point. That is
correct for each: G1 and G01 denote the same command, so an integer normalises them, while a
coordinate of 12.5 must keep its fraction.

sR = float(np.mean([rev[i][1] for i in probe]))

idx = list(range(n))[::-1]
return ([np.rot90(crops[i], 2) for i in idx], [out[i][0] for i in idx],

def _RenderOneGlyph(g,cell=90,pad=8):
strokes = g.get("strokes",[])
im = Image.new("L",(cell,cell),255)
draw = ImageDraw.Draw(im)
allpts = [p for s in strokes for p in s]
if not allpts:
return im
xs = [p[0] for p in allpts]
ys = [p[1] for p in allpts]
x0,x1,y0,y1 = min(xs),max(xs),min(ys),max(ys)
w = max(x1-x0,0.01)
h = max(y1-y0,0.01)
scale = (cell-2*pad)/max(w,h)
def tx(p):
return (pad+(p[0]-x0)*scale,cell-pad-(p[1]-y0)*scale)
for s in strokes:
pts = [tx(p) for p in s]
if len(pts)>=2:
draw.line(pts,fill=0,width=2)
return im

15.1 Expanded reasoning: data partitions, loss derivatives and training

15.1.1 The 15% holdout, seed and 20% personal representation
The inspected paths specify validation fraction 0.15 and split seed zero. A seeded shuffle fixes which
examples are withheld, provided the example list and ordering are unchanged. The fraction controls
data allocation; the seed controls reproducibility, not statistical quality. For a constructed 100-line
population a 15% split with exact rounding gives 15 validation and 85 training lines. Real per-writer
rounding and minimum-set guards can change totals. Never infer actual held-out counts from the
fraction alone.
A line-level split can put neighbouring lines from one photographed page in both sets. This tests
new lines under partly shared capture conditions, not new pages, pens or writers. A page-level split
reduces that dependency; a writer-disjoint split answers a different question from closed-set writer
identification. Fifteen percent is a sample-efficiency/precision compromise, not a statistically universal
optimum. After tuning on validation, it no longer serves as a fully untouched final test.
The text trainer’s personal fraction 0.20 controls representation during mixed sampling [3]. It
does not make public and personal data equal: the intended shares are 80/20. In an ideal twenty-
example batch, that would mean sixteen public and four personal examples, subject to the routine’s
rounding/replacement behaviour. Oversampling a small personal set can repeat examples; an epoch
need not then mean one visit per unique image. This coefficient is separate from 0.2 dropout and
from the 15% holdout. Its rationale is to prevent abundant public data overwhelming the personal
domain; it does not guarantee absence of bias or optimum transfer.

deformation [22]. It assumes the label is unchanged. An excessive warp can violate that assumption

def UnfilterPng(raw,height,stride,bpp):
out = np.zeros((height,stride),dtype=np.uint8)
prev = np.zeros(stride,dtype=np.uint8)
pos = 0
for r in range(height):
ft = raw[pos]
line = np.frombuffer(raw,dtype=np.uint8,count=stride,offset=pos+1)
pos += 1+stride
if ft==0:
cur = line.copy()
elif ft==1: #sub: a running total along the row
if bpp==1:
cur = (np.cumsum(line,dtype=np.int64)&255).astype(np.uint8)
else:
pad = (-stride)%bpp
wide = np.concatenate([line.astype(np.int64),np.zeros(pad,dtype=np.int64)])
cur = (np.cumsum(wide.reshape(-1,bpp),axis=0).reshape(-1)[:stride]&255
).astype(np.uint8)
elif ft==2: #up: add the row above, wrapping at 256
cur = line+prev
else:
cur = bytearray(line)
pv = prev.tobytes()
if ft==3: #average of left and above
for i in range(min(bpp,stride)):
cur[i] = (cur[i]+(pv[i]>>1))&255
for i in range(bpp,stride):
cur[i] = (cur[i]+((cur[i-bpp]+pv[i])>>1))&255
else: #paeth: whichever neighbour predicts best
for i in range(min(bpp,stride)):
cur[i] = (cur[i]+pv[i])&255
for i in range(bpp,stride):
a,b,c = cur[i-bpp],pv[i],pv[i-bpp]
est = a+b-c
da,db,dc = abs(est-a),abs(est-b),abs(est-c)
cur[i] = (cur[i]+(a if (da<=db and da<=dc) else (b if db<=dc else c)))&255
cur = np.frombuffer(bytes(cur),dtype=np.uint8)
out[r] = cur
prev = cur
return out

body = data[i+8:i+8+length]

if bitDepth!=8 or interlace!=0:

def BuildHuffTable(counts,values):
minCode = [0]*17
maxCode = [-1]*17
valPtr = [0]*17
code = k = 0
lut = np.full(256,-1,dtype=np.int32)
lutLen = np.zeros(256,dtype=np.uint8)
for length in range(1,17):
valPtr[length] = k
minCode[length] = code
for _ in range(counts[length-1]):
if length<=8:
base = code<<(8-length)
for fill in range(1<<(8-length)):
lut[base+fill] = values[k]
lutLen[base+fill] = length
code += 1
k += 1
maxCode[length] = code-1
code <<= 1
return dict(minCode=minCode,maxCode=maxCode,valPtr=valPtr,values=values,
lut=lut,lutLen=lutLen)

def DecodeHuffValue(reader,table):
peek = reader.Peek8()
length = int(table["lutLen"][peek])
if length:
reader.Skip(length)
return int(table["lut"][peek])
code = 0
for length in range(1,17):
code = (code<<1)|reader.Receive(1)
if code<=table["maxCode"][length]:
return table["values"][table["valPtr"][length]+code-table["minCode"][length]]
raise ValueError("bad huffman code")

Justification | Why crops are cached at all
Extracting line crops from a page is slow: the page must be read, binarised, analysed for line positions

into a single file and read back by offset. Storing each crop as a separate image file would mean tens

whole block to a file however small.

Justification | Why the transcript is per line rather than per page
The reader works on one line at a time, so each crop needs its own label. Keeping the transcript as
one line of text per line of writing means the correspondence is positional: the n-th transcript line
labels the n-th crop. That is what makes it possible to check the extraction, since a page whose crop
count does not match its transcript line count has been segmented wrongly and can be rejected rather
than silently mislabelled.
Deriving the transcript’s path from the image’s by convention, rather than being told it, is what
lets a directory of pages be processed by listing the images alone. The cost is that the convention is
implicit: a transcript named differently is simply not found, and the page is skipped.

Purpose | What it is for
Given a set of interesting rows, such as those containing a printed rule, groups the ones that are
close together. A single printed line a few pixels thick registers as several adjacent rows, and what is
wanted is one entry per rule rather than one per row.
Method | The rule
The indices are taken in order and a new cluster is started whenever the gap to the previous one
exceeds the limit. This is single-link clustering in one dimension, and it is the natural formulation
when the data is ordered: two rows belong together if they are close, and closeness chains, so a run of
rows each near the last forms one cluster however long it is.
A gap of five pixels suits the printed rules on ruled paper, which are a pixel or two thick with
occasional breaks where writing crosses them. The chaining property is what bridges those breaks,
and it is also the method’s weakness: a dense enough sequence of separate features merges into one
cluster.

locate characters rather than to recognise them.

the right number of pieces passes, and its labels are then confidently wrong. The count is a necessary
condition for a correct extraction, not a sufficient one.

Justification | The approach, and why periodicity is the right tool
Lines of writing on a page are close to evenly spaced, because the writer followed the ruling or kept a
steady hand. That regularity is strong evidence and it is what the splitter uses: rather than looking
for each gap independently, it establishes the pitch and then expects boundaries at roughly that
spacing.
The advantage over independent gap-finding is robustness to a single bad gap. A line whose descenders
reach into the next line leaves almost no gap at all, and a method looking only for gaps misses that
boundary entirely, merging two lines. A method that knows the expected spacing looks for a boundary
where one ought to be and places it at the best available row, even where that row is not a clear gap.
Justification | Why the printed rules are used as hints
Where the ruling was found, it says where the writer intended each line to sit, which is better evidence
than the ink profile: it is unaffected by descenders, by a line of unusual height, or by a blank line.
The hints are used to guide the boundaries rather than to set them, because writers do not follow
ruling exactly.
This whole routine is a separate, earlier solution to the problem segment.py solves with seam carving.
The seam approach is better, since it cuts around descenders instead of choosing a row to cut
through. This one remains because it is what the cached training data was extracted with, and
re-extracting it would change the data the reported checkpoints were trained on.

than once per epoch.
Justification | Why one file with an index
Tens of thousands of separate image files would be slow, because each open is a separate filesystem
operation, and wasteful, because a filesystem allocates a whole block per file. One file read at an
offset is a single operation, and the index is small enough to hold in memory.

The extracted crops for the full database run to several gigabytes, more than is comfortable to hold
while also holding the activations a training step needs. Reading each crop as the batch needs it keeps
the memory use to the batch, and the operating system’s own file cache keeps the recently used parts
in memory anyway, which recovers most of the speed without the program managing it.

Justification | Why the order is shuffled for training
The examples arrive grouped by page and therefore by writer. Without shuffling, consecutive batches
would each contain one writer’s hand, so the network would be pulled toward that hand and then
away from it, which both slows convergence and makes the loss oscillate with the data order rather
than with learning. Shuffling makes each batch an approximately representative sample, which is the
assumption the gradient estimate rests on.
Justification | Why validation is not shuffled
Validation computes a mean over the whole set, and a mean does not depend on the order. Keeping
the order fixed makes the measurement exactly reproducible between runs, which matters when
comparing two checkpoints: any difference is then attributable to the weights rather than to the
batching.

Batches are produced one at a time rather than built as a list, so only the current batch is in
memory. For a dataset of tens of thousands of crops that is the difference between a few hundred
megabytes and several gigabytes.

Justification | Why a held-out set is necessary
Training loss falls whether or not the network is learning anything general, because a network with
enough capacity can memorise its training examples. The only way to tell memorisation from learning
is to measure on data the network has never been trained on. That is theheld-outor validation set,
and the gap between training and validation loss is the measure of overfitting.
Justification | Why two numbers are reported
The loss and the character accuracy answer different questions, and both are needed. The loss is what
training minimises, so it is the quantity the scheduler and the best-checkpoint logic must use, and it
is sensitive to small changes in confidence. Character accuracy is what anyone actually cares about,
but it is coarse: a network can improve its loss substantially with no change in accuracy, because it
has become more confident about answers it already had right.
Augmentation is off here, through the evaluation view, and batch normalisation uses its stored
statistics, through the evaluation forward pass. Both are necessary for the measurement to describe
the checkpoint that will be saved rather than some variant of it.

rather than four times, which matters because each resampling blurs it slightly.
The order reads right to left, since the rightmost matrix acts on the point first. That is the usual
convention for column-vector coordinates and it is the opposite of the order the operations are listed
in prose.

The combined matrix is inverted before being used. The reason is the direction resampling works
in: for eachoutputpixel, the warp asks which input position it came from, which is the inverse map.
Working forward instead, pushing each input pixel to its output position, leaves gaps where no input
pixel happens to land and collisions where two do. Working backwards fills every output pixel exactly
once, which is why it is universal in image warping. The same argument appears under Warp in
segment.py.

Slant is one source of writer and page variation. Shear augmentation exposes training to changed

The division by a function of position is what distinguishes it from an affine map and what makes
parallel lines converge: points further away in the implied depth direction are divided by a larger

Four corner correspondences are given, each fixing two equations, giving eight equations for the
eight unknowns. The equations above are not linear in the coefficients because of the division, but
multiplying each through by its denominator makes them linear, and that rearrangement is what the
rows of the matrix in the code are: each row is one such multiplied-out equation, with the cross terms
carrying the negative signs the rearrangement produces.
The resulting system is then solved by standard linear algebra. The reason four corners are exactly right
is that eight unknowns need eight equations: three corners would leave the system underdetermined
and five would overdetermine it, requiring a least-squares fit rather than a solution.

Output.the crop with a smooth random warp applied.
Method | What it simulates
Elastic distortion[22] displaces every pixel by a small smoothly varying random amount, so the
image is stretched here and compressed there. For handwriting it imitates the natural variation of
a hand: the same person writing the same word twice produces shapes that differ in just this way,
locally stretched and squeezed rather than globally transformed.
Justification | How the smoothness is obtained, and why it is essential
Two random displacement fields are generated, one per axis, and each is blurred with a Gaussian before
being applied. The blurring is what makes the method work. An unblurred random displacement
moves each pixel independently, which is simply noise: it destroys the strokes rather than deforming
them. After blurring, nearby pixels move together, so a stroke stays a connected stroke and is merely
bent.
The blur width therefore controls the character of the distortion. A wide blur gives a nearly uniform
displacement, which is just a translation; a narrow one approaches noise. The useful range is a width
comparable to the features being deformed, which for handwriting is around a letter’s size. The
amplitude scales the displacement after blurring, since blurring reduces the magnitude as well as
smoothing it.

The reasoning runs as follows. An output is a sum of fanIn products of a weight and an input. For
independent terms, variances add, so the output’s variance is fanIn times the product of the weight
and input variances. Keeping the output’s variance equal to the input’s therefore requires the weight
variance to be one over fanIn. That is the Glorot argument [84].
The factor of 2 is the correction for ReLU [83]. ReLU sets every negative value to zero, discarding
about half the signal’s variance, so without compensation the variance would halve at every layer and
after twelve layers be reduced by a factor of four thousand. Doubling the weight variance exactly
offsets it. The difference between the two initialisations is only that factor, and for a network this
deep it is the difference between training and not.
Justification | Why the bias starts at zero
There is nothing to break symmetry in a bias, because the weights are already random, so each unit
already computes something different. Zero is the neutral starting point, and it is also harmless here
because the batch normalisation that follows removes any constant offset anyway, as noted under
ConvBlockForward.

Justification | Why the scale starts at one and the shift at zero
Those values make the learned part of the layer the identity: the output is the standardised input
unchanged. So the layer begins by doing exactly the normalisation it exists for and nothing else, and
any departure from that is something training chose. Starting the scale at a random value would add
a per-channel distortion the network would have to learn to undo before making progress.
Justification | Why the running statistics start at zero and one
A mean of zero and a variance of one describe already-standardised data, so a network evaluated
before any training behaves as though normalisation had been applied correctly. They are also the
values the exponential average converges away from fastest: being the neutral assumption, any real
data moves them in a meaningful direction immediately.
These two pairs are treated differently everywhere else in the file. The scale and shift are parameters
with gradients and are updated by the optimiser; the running statistics have no gradients and
are updated by observation. TrainableParams separates them by name, which is why the naming
convention for them is load-bearing.

The arithmetic is identical to Conv2d in recognise.py, including the im2col rearrangement and the
strided view, both explained in that entry. The only difference is that this one keeps a cache.
Justification | What is cached, and why each item is needed
• The input’s shape,not the input itself. The backward pass builds a gradient array of that
shape and never needs the values.
• The weights,because the input gradient is formed by multiplying the output gradient by
them.
• The flattened columns,which is the significant one. The weight gradient is the output
gradient multiplied by exactly these patches, so keeping them avoids rebuilding them, which
would mean redoing the strided view and the reshape.
• The padding and the filter and output sizes,so the backward pass can fold the column
gradient back into image shape without recomputing the geometry.
Justification | The cost of caching, and why it is accepted
The columns are the memory cost of training. A 3 by 3 filter over three channels makes each patch 27
numbers, and there is one patch per output position, so the cached columns are roughly nine times
the size of the input feature map. Every convolution in the network holds its own for the whole
forward pass, since none can be released until the backward pass has used it. That, rather than the
weights, is what sets the largest batch size that fits in memory, and it is why training needs far more
memory than inference.
No bias-related value is cached. The bias gradient is just the output gradient summed over every
position, which needs nothing from the forward pass, because adding a constant has a derivative of
one.

Method | The channel progression
One channel in, then 32, then 64, then 128, with two, four and six groups in the three stages. The

Justification | Why that arrangement
Two reasons, one about capacity and one about cost. Deeper layers represent larger and more varied

large structures than small ones, so more channels are needed to hold them. And since each pooling
quarters the spatial size, doubling the channels leaves the work per layer roughly halved rather than
growing, so the deeper stages are affordable despite being wider and having more groups.

Both the reader and the namer use exactly this backbone, initialised by this one function. The
features useful for recognising a letter and for recognising a hand are largely the same features, as
argued under AuthorClassifierCNNNumpy, so there is no reason for the two to differ, and sharing the
initialiser means a change to the architecture applies to both rather than to one.

15.81 Method background: Training dropout and expectation scaling
Purpose | The role in this system
Randomly mask hidden responses during training and preserve their expected scale.
Justification | The reason for this construction
Inverted dropout divides retained responses by their keep probability. This discourages reliance on
one particular activation combination; inference uses the unmasked network.
Alternatives | What changes if another method is used
No dropout removes this source of training noise. Weight decay penalises parameter magnitude and
image augmentation changes inputs; these regularisers act differently and can be combined.
Library | Implementation speed and accuracy
A framework dropout layer handles train/eval switching and random masks. Match keep probability,
mask shape, dtype and random seed for a numerical comparison. It adds no inference-time masking
when disabled; it does not guarantee higher held-out accuracy. [43, 3].

probabilities add because they are mutually exclusive ways of the same thing happening.
Summing is also what makes CTC trainable at all. If training used the maximum it would be
committing to one alignment and pushing the network toward it, which would be arbitrary early on
when the network has no idea where anything is. Summing lets the network be rewarded for any
layout that spells the right text, and the alignment emerges from training rather than being imposed.

why that function exists.

The second term is called theoccupation: among all the alignments that spell the target, the

already agrees with the occupation the gradient is zero; where it predicts too much of a class the

gradient a difference, and it arises for the same reason: the softmax and the logarithm in the loss
are inverse operations, so differentiating their composition cancels the awkward terms. It is why the
gradient is computed with respect to the raw logits rather than with respect to the log probabilities,
even though the loss was defined on the latter: taking the whole softmax and loss together is far
simpler than either separately.
Justification | Why there is a loop over the batch
Each example has its own label and so its own length of extended sequence, so the dynamic
programming tables are different shapes and cannot be computed as one array. The loop over
the batch is therefore unavoidable, and inside it the loops over time and over states remain in Python
too, which makes this the slowest function in the file. The small loop over states checking the skip
restriction could be vectorised by precomputing the mask once per example instead of once per
column, which is the obvious remaining optimisation.
Both the loss and the gradient are divided by the batch size, so the loss is a mean over examples
rather than a total. That makes it comparable between batch sizes, which matters because the
learning rate is tuned against the gradient’s magnitude: without the division, doubling the batch
size would double the gradient and effectively double the learning rate.
Stage: Writer cross entropy
15.89 Method background: Writer cross entropy
Purpose | The role in this system
Penalise the network for assigning low probability to the labelled writer.
Justification | The reason for this construction
For a one-hot writer label, negative log probability is the categorical negative log likelihood. Its logit
gradient is predicted probability minus the target indicator; it trains the mutually exclusive writer
head.
Alternatives | What changes if another method is used
Squared probability error changes the derivative and optimisation behaviour. Class-weighted cross
entropy changes the relative cost of examples and needs a justified weighting policy. This is distinct
from CTC, which marginalises unknown character alignments.
Library | Implementation speed and accuracy
Framework cross-entropy losses normally accept raw logits and combine stable log softmax with target
indexing. Feeding probabilities instead, or changing sum/mean reduction, changes the objective or
gradient scale. A compiled loss may reduce overhead but is not inherently a different classifier. [48, 3].

ReLU is the identity where the input was positive and constant zero where it was not, so its derivative
is one or zero accordingly. The backward pass is therefore the incoming gradient with the inactive
positions zeroed: the gradient passes unchanged through the units that fired and stops dead at the
ones that did not.
Justification | Why this is the property that makes deep networks trainable
A derivative of exactly 1 on the active path is what distinguishes ReLU from the smooth activations
it replaced. The sigmoid’s derivative is at most 0.25 and much smaller when saturated, so a gradient
crossing twelve sigmoid layers is multiplied by twelve such factors and arrives at the first layer
effectively zero. That is the vanishing gradient problem, and it is why networks of this depth were
impractical before ReLU. With a factor of exactly 1 the gradient reaches the first layer at full strength.
The derivative at exactly zero does not exist, since the function has a corner there. Taking it as
zero is conventional and the choice has no practical consequence: an input of exactly zero is a
measure-zero event in floating point, and either choice gives a valid subgradient.

magnitude and scrambled in position, which trains to something, slowly and wrongly, without any
error being raised. It is exactly the kind of fault the numerical gradient check exists to catch.

Method | The reversal

activation, then normalisation, then convolution. Each step takes the gradient from the step before it,

use. That is what lets the optimiser be written without any knowledge of the network’s structure: it
iterates over the parameters and looks up each one’s gradient by name. The names are therefore a
contract between three separate things, the initialiser, the backward pass and the checkpoint format,
and a mismatch in any of them fails with a missing key rather than silently training the wrong array.
The variable holding the gradient is reassigned at each step rather than being given a new name per
layer. That reads oddly but is exactly right: there is only ever one gradient travelling backwards at
a time, and naming its successive values separately would suggest they coexist.

Every line is the product rule: the gradient with respect to one factor is the incoming gradient times
the other factor. The cell gradient has two contributions because the cell is used twice, revealed
through the hidden state at this step and carried forward to the next, which is the same double-use
argument as for the hidden state.

The last line is worth isolating. The gradient carried back to the previous cell state is the current
cell gradient multiplied by the forget gate, and by nothing else: no weight matrix is applied along
this path. So if the forget gate is near 1, the gradient passes backwards through that step essentially
unchanged, and it can do so for many steps in succession without shrinking.
That is the precise sense in which the LSTM solves the vanishing gradient problem. A plain recurrent
layer multiplies the carried gradient by its recurrent weight matrix at every step, so after a hundred
steps it has been multiplied by that matrix a hundred times and is either negligible or enormous. The
LSTM’s cell path multiplies only by gate values the network itself controls, and it can learn to set
them near 1 where information must survive.
Method | Through the squashing functions
Each gate gradient is then passed back through its own activation to reach the pre-activation value,
which is what the weights actually produced. For the three sigmoid gates the derivative is the output
times one minus the output, and for the candidate it is one minus the output squared. Both are
written in terms of the output rather than the input, which is why the cache holds the gate activations
and not the pre-activations.
Method | The weight gradients
The four pre-activation gradients are concatenated back into the stacked layout the weights use,
and the weight gradients are then matrix products of that stack with the step’s input and previous
hidden state. They are accumulated across steps with addition rather than assignment, which is the
shared-parameter sum. Both biases receive the same gradient, since both were added to the same
quantity, which is the backward counterpart of the inference note that only their sum has any effect.
The input gradient is written per step into a preallocated array rather than appended, because
the steps are visited in reverse and the result must come back in forward order. Appending and
reversing would also work; writing by index makes the ordering explicit at the point it matters.

Method | Splitting the gradient
The forward pass concatenated the two directions along the feature axis, so the incoming gradient is
split at the same point: the first half belongs to the forward direction and the second to the backward
one. Concatenation and splitting are exact inverses, so no arithmetic is involved.
Justification | Why the two input gradients are added
Both directions read thesameinput sequence, so the input is a shared quantity and by the shared-
parameter rule its gradient is the sum of the two directions’ contributions. This is easy to get wrong
by treating them as separate inputs and returning only one, which halves the gradient reaching the
convolutional backbone and makes it train at half rate with no visible symptom.
Method | The reversal, undone
The backward direction’s gradient must be reversed before being handed to its LSTM backward pass
and reversed again afterwards, mirroring the two reversals of the forward pass. The invariant to hold
on to is that every array crossing the boundary of this function is in forward time order, and the
reversed order exists only inside it.

Purpose | The problem plain gradient descent has
A single learning rate must suit every weight, and it cannot. Different weights have gradients of wildly
different magnitudes, by orders of magnitude between layers and between a bias and a convolution
weight. A rate small enough to be stable for the largest gradients is far too small for the smallest, so
some weights barely move while others oscillate.
Method | The idea: divide by the typical gradient size
RMSprop[ 89] keeps, for each weight, a running average of its squared gradient, and divides the
step by the square root of that. A weight whose gradients are habitually large is divided by a large
number and takes a small step; one with habitually small gradients takes a comparatively large one.
The effect is that every weight moves at a comparable rate regardless of its gradient’s scale.

Justification | Why the averages must be bias-corrected
Both averages start at zero, which is not a neutral starting point but a strong claim that the gradient
is zero. After one step the first moment is only one tenth of the observed gradient, and the second is
one thousandth of its square, so early steps would be far too small and, worse, badly misproportioned
between the two, since they are biased by different amounts.
The correction divides each by one minus its decay raised to the step number, which is exactly
the total weight the average has accumulated so far. At step 1 the first moment is divided by 0.1,
recovering the full gradient; by step 100 the divisor is nearly 1 and the correction fades away. So the
optimiser behaves sensibly from its very first step, which matters because the first steps are taken
from random weights where large corrections are most needed.
Justification | Why the W, and what it fixes
Weight decayshrinks every weight slightly at each step, which discourages large weights and reduces
overfitting. Classically it is implemented by adding a multiple of the weight to its gradient, which for
plain gradient descent is exactly equivalent.
With Adam it is not equivalent, and that is the point of AdamW [81]. A decay term added to
the gradient passes through the division by the square-root average like any other gradient, so a
weight with large gradients has its decay divided down and is barely regularised, while one with small
gradients is decayed heavily. The strength of the regularisation therefore varies per weight in a way
nobody intended, and it depends on the gradient history rather than on the weight.
The fix is to apply the decay to the weight directly, outside the scaled step, which is the separate term
in the update above. Every weight is then shrunk by the same proportion, which is what weight decay
is supposed to mean. This is calleddecoupledweight decay, and the W in the name stands for it.

rate, so the effective decay changes as the learning rate is annealed. The original formulation
decouples it from the learning rate as well. The difference matters mainly late in training, when
the rate has fallen and the decay falls with it.

Justification | Why the learning rate should change during training
A large rate is right early on, when the weights are far from any good configuration and large steps
make rapid progress. It is wrong later, when the weights are close and a large step jumps past the
minimum and bounces around it. So the rate should start large and end small, and ascheduleris
what changes it.
Method | This scheduler’s rule
It watches a metric, usually the validation loss, and remembers the best value seen. Each epoch that
fails to beat the best counts as a bad epoch; once the bad epochs exceed the patience, the learning
rate is multiplied by the factor and the count resets. A new best resets it too.
Justification | Why it reacts rather than following a schedule
The advantage over a fixed schedule is that it needs no estimate of how long training will take. It
lowers the rate exactly when progress has stopped, which is the evidence that the current rate is
now too large, whatever epoch that happens to be. The disadvantage is that it only reacts after the
patience has elapsed, so several epochs are spent at a rate already known to be too large.
Justification | Why the patience is needed
Validation loss is noisy, because it is measured on a finite set and the weights change between epochs.
A single epoch failing to improve means little. Requiring five consecutive failures distinguishes a
genuine plateau from the ordinary fluctuation of a metric that is still improving overall. Too little
patience lowers the rate on noise and ends training early at a rate too small to make progress.
The floor on the learning rate stops the repeated halving from reaching zero, at which point training
would continue indefinitely without changing anything. It is a way of bounding wasted time rather
than a property of the method.

means the learning rate or the limit is wrong, and a sudden spike identifies the batch that caused it.
Without the return value, clipping would silently conceal the very instability it is protecting against.

Justification | What it excludes and why
The running mean and variance of every batch normalisation. They are stored alongside the parameters,
because they must be saved in the checkpoint, but they are not parameters: no gradient is computed
for them, and they are updated by observing the data rather than by descending a loss.
Method | What would happen if they were included
The optimiser would look up a gradient for them, find none, and fail with a missing key, which is the
benign outcome. Had a zero gradient been supplied instead, the optimiser would apply weight decay
to them and shrink them steadily toward zero, so the stored variances would fall and inference would
divide by a smaller and smaller number, amplifying every activation. That is a silent corruption
which would appear only at inference, as a network whose validation accuracy during training was
fine and whose saved checkpoint performs badly.
The separation is by name suffix, which works but ties correctness to a naming convention. A
parameter accidentally named with one of those suffixes would be silently frozen, and one of these
accidentally named otherwise would be silently decayed.

Method | What goes into a checkpoint
Every parameter, including the running statistics, plus metadata: which epoch it came from and the

Justification | Why the metadata must be in the file
Resuming a run requires knowing which epoch to continue from and what the best loss was, so that

those in the checkpoint rather than in a separate file means they cannot be separated from the weights

silently misschedules the learning rate.

uses to tell metadata from weights. The two functions are in different files and must agree on it,
which is worth noting as another implicit contract.

interrupted run leaves a readable log ending at the last finished epoch, where a rewritten file could be

17.14 Additional vocabulary needed to defend the calculations
Dimensionless coefficient.
A pure ratio or multiplier without units. Its numerical effect still depends on the scale of the
quantity it multiplies. Changing cost normalisation can change a coefficient’s meaning.
Heuristic versus hyperparameter.
A heuristic is a practical rule without a general optimality guarantee. A hyperparameter is a
setting chosen outside ordinary weight learning. A setting can be both. A learned convolution
weight is a model parameter; dropout probability is a hyperparameter.
Guard, floor, cap and clamp.
A guard handles an invalid or exceptional case; a floor enforces a minimum; a cap enforces a
maximum; clipping enforces both. A numerical guard prevents arithmetic failure, not necessarily
bad input.
Quantile and percentile.
A quantileqf marks fractionf of a distribution; a percentile expresses100f. The 60th percentile
is not 60% of the maximum. Interpolation conventions can differ on small samples.
424

Handwriting Robot Code theory DemoCode edition
Argmax and argmin.
They return the location/index attaining an extreme, not the extreme value. Ties require a
rule, often first occurrence.
Indicator.
1[E]is one if statementE is true and zero otherwise. It encodes a decision without implying a
probability.
Recurrence, state and backtracking.
A recurrence computes new entries from previous ones. A state summarises what a prefix needs
for future choices. Backtracking follows saved choices to recover a path. A recurrence can sum
paths, as CTC does, or optimise one path, as a seam/alignment does.
Dynamic programming versus greedy choice.
Dynamic programming compares prefix solutions for each state; a greedy rule takes an immediate
best choice. Both can be fast, but they solve different optimisation problems.
Prior and posterior.
A prior expresses information before a particular observation; a posterior conditions on it. The
project’s glyph “prior” is a pooled geometric reference, not a fully specified Bayesian probability
distribution. CTC state occupancy is a conditional path posterior under the model and target.
Likelihood versus confidence.
Likelihood evaluates observations/labels under a model. A softmax output is normalised model
confidence; its match to real frequencies requires calibration evidence. High confidence can be
wrong.
Calibration, two meanings.
Mechanical calibration relates pulse counts to reference positions/lengths. Probability calibration
relates predicted confidence to observed frequency. The procedures and units are unrelated.
Bias and variance, two contexts.
Measurement bias is systematic offset; sampling variance is variation across repeated estimates.
A neural bias is an additive learned parameter. An unbiased variance estimator is a statistical
formula, not a guarantee a classifier is fair or accurate.
Regularisation and weight decay.
Regularisation constrains learning to reduce overfitting. Weight decay shrinks parameters.
Dropout, augmentation, early selection and penalties influence generalisation by different
mechanisms; their strengths cannot simply be added as one scalar percentage.
Epoch, update and iteration.
An update changes parameters after a batch; an iteration may mean one such processing step;
an epoch follows the sampler’s definition of a pass. Replacement/mixture sampling can revisit
images within one epoch. A checkpoint’s epoch index is not elapsed time.
Logit and log probability.
A logit is an unrestricted score. Log-softmax subtracts log-sum-exp to produce log probabilities.
Log probabilities are nonpositive; logits need not be. Exponentiating an arbitrary logit alone is
not a normalised probability.
Jacobian, gradient and chain rule.
A Jacobian contains derivatives of vector outputs with respect to vector inputs. A scalar loss
gradient is the corresponding vector derivative. Backpropagation efficiently composes these
derivatives without storing every full Jacobian.
425

Handwriting Robot Code theory DemoCode edition
Subgradient.
A selected derivative-like value at a nonsmooth point. ReLU at zero and max ties require
conventions; disagreement there is not necessarily evidence of an incorrect smooth derivative
elsewhere.
Float32, float64 and tolerance.
Floating-point types have finite precision, not exact real arithmetic. Comparison tolerance
defines an allowed discrepancy for a particular scale. A tolerance is neither a p-value nor a
physical instrument uncertainty.
Isotropic versus anisotropic.
Isotropic scaling uses one factor in both axes; anisotropic scaling uses different factors and
changes aspect ratio. Normalisation describes a transformation, not proof that remaining
differences are exclusively writer style.
Aliasing and interpolation.
Aliasing occurs when sampled detail becomes indistinguishable from another pattern. Interpola-
tion estimates intermediate values but cannot reliably recreate information lost by undersampling.
Antialiasing before reduction limits high-frequency content to reduce this risk.
Topology versus geometry.
Topology concerns connections, components and holes; geometry concerns positions, lengths
and angles. Small geometric error does not necessarily preserve a tiny loop, and a connected
skeleton can still have poor geometric fidelity.
Open-loop versus feedback.
Open-loop axis control estimates position from commands. Feedback observes a quantity, such
as an endstop or pen-up switch. Having some switches does not make every interior carriage
position closed-loop or verify pen pressure.
Resolution, repeatability, accuracy and uncertainty.
Resolution is the smallest represented/readable increment. Repeatability describes consistency
under repeated conditions. Accuracy concerns agreement with a reference. Uncertainty charac-
terises the range attributable to measurement knowledge. A fine step lattice alone establishes
none of the other three.
Macro and micro aggregation.
Macro gives each group equal weight; micro pools elementary counts. Equal-writer ratios, word
means and pooled character counts therefore answer different questions even on the same files.
Ablation and sensitivity.
Ablation removes a mechanism to assess its contribution under controlled conditions. Sensitivity
varies a setting and observes response. A sensitivity plot can reveal fragility without proving a
global optimum. No such new execution is part of this edition.
Confusion matrix.
Rows/columns count actual/predicted class pairs. Row normalisation divides by actual-class
counts, showing conditional prediction fractions. It does not equal class precision, which uses
predicted-class totals. An overall average without counts can conceal class imbalance.
Selection leakage and provenance.
Selection leakage occurs when a test set influences tuning and is later presented as untouched.
Provenance records where an input, model or number came from. It prevents an old result from
being silently attributed to a newer code revision or different host.

18 Glossary
Terms used in this manual, in plain language. They are grouped by subject rather than alphabetically,
because reading a group in order explains more than reading a definition on its own.
18.1 Arrays and arithmetic
Array
A grid of numbers. A one-dimensional array is a list, a two-dimensional array is a table, and
a greyscale image is a two-dimensional array where each number is the brightness of one pixel,
usually from 0 for black to 255 for white.
Element-wise
An operation applied to every number in an array independently. Adding 10 to an image,
element-wise, makes every pixel ten levels brighter.
Vectorised
Written so that an operation is applied to a whole array at once rather than by looping over the
elements one at a time in Python. This matters for speed: the loop runs inside compiled code
instead of in the interpreter, which is typically between ten and a hundred times faster.
Cumulative sum, or prefix sum
An array where each entry is the total of everything up to that point. For the input(2, 3, 1, 4)the
cumulative sum is(2, 5, 6, 10). Its usefulness is that the total of any stretch of the original can
then be found by one subtraction, because the total fromi to j equals the entry atj minus the
entry ati.
Mask
An array of true and false values, used to mark which pixels belong to something. An “ink mask”
is true at every pixel judged to be ink and false elsewhere.
Dot product
For two lists of equal length, the sum of the products of corresponding entries. If both lists are
first scaled so that their own length is one, the dot product equals the cosine of the angle between
them considered as arrows, which is why it is used in this project to measure how similar two
shapes are.
Norm
The length of a list of numbers considered as an arrow from the origin, which is the square root of
the sum of the squares of its entries.
Interpolation
Estimating a value between known values. If a transformed image needs the brightness at a
position halfway between two pixels, interpolation supplies it as a blend of the neighbours.
Median
The middle value when a set of numbers is sorted. It is used throughout this project in preference
to the mean (the ordinary average) because it is insensitive to a small number of extreme values:
one badly wrong measurement among eleven good ones moves the mean but not the median.
Percentile
The value below which a given share of the data falls. The 40th percentile is the value that 40 per
cent of the data lies below. The median is the 50th percentile.
428

Handwriting Robot Code theory DemoCode edition
Variance and standard deviation
Measures of how spread out a set of numbers is. The variance is the average of the squared
distances from the mean; the standard deviation is its square root, which has the same units as
the data.
18.2 Images and shapes
Threshold
A brightness level used to divide an image into two groups, typically ink and paper. “Thresholding”
is applying it.
Histogram
A count of how many pixels fall at each brightness level. It describes an image’s distribution of
tones without reference to where anything is.
Morphology
A family of operations that change the shapes in a mask rather than the values in an image:
growing shapes, shrinking them, filling small holes, removing small specks.
Structuring element, or kernel
The small window a morphological or filtering operation looks through. A square kernel of radius
2 is a five-by-five window centred on each pixel.
Dilation and erosion
Growing and shrinking shapes. Dilation turns a pixel on if anything nearby is on; erosion turns it
off unless everything nearby is on.
Closing
A dilation followed by an erosion by the same amount. The net effect is that small gaps are bridged
while the overall thickness of a shape is preserved.
Connected component
A group of pixels that touch one another, treated as a single object. A letter, a dot over ani and
a speck of dust are each a connected component.
Connectivity
Which neighbours count as touching. Four-connectivity counts only the pixels above, below, left
and right; eight-connectivity also counts the four diagonals, so two pixels meeting at a corner
belong to the same component.
Skeleton, or centreline
A one-pixel-wide line running down the middle of a thick stroke. Thinning a pen stroke to its
skeleton recovers approximately the path the pen travelled.
Projection profile
The result of adding up the ink in each row, or in each column, producing a one-dimensional
summary of a two-dimensional image. Lines of text appear as peaks in the row profile.
Polyline
A path described by an ordered list of points, understood to be joined by straight segments.
Aspect ratio
The ratio of width to height.
Bounding box
The smallest upright rectangle containing a shape.
429

Handwriting Robot Code theory DemoCode edition
18.3 Networks and training
Neural network
A function with a very large number of adjustable numbers, called weights, arranged in layers.
Each layer takes the output of the previous one and performs a simple operation; the composition
can represent complicated relationships. Training is the process of adjusting the weights so the
function gives the right answers on examples.
Weight and bias
The adjustable numbers. A weight multiplies an input; a bias is added afterwards. Together they
are the parameters.
Layer
One stage of a network.
Feature map
The output of a convolutional layer: an array showing, for each position in the image, how strongly
some learned pattern was detected there.
Channel
One such map. A layer producing 64 channels is detecting 64 different patterns.
Convolution
Sliding a small grid of weights over an image and recording the response at every position, which
detects the same pattern wherever it occurs.
Activation function
A simple non-linear function applied after a layer, such as setting negatives to zero. Without one,
stacking layers would be pointless, because a chain of purely linear operations is equivalent to a
single linear operation.
Pooling
Reducing the size of a feature map by summarising each small window, typically by its largest
value, which saves work and makes the result tolerant to small shifts.
Logit
A raw score produced by the final layer, before it is converted into a probability. Logits may be
any real number, positive or negative.
Softmax
The conversion from logits to probabilities: exponentiate each score and divide by the total, which
forces them to be positive and to sum to one.
Loss function
A single number measuring how wrong the network’s output is on a training example. Training
consists of reducing it.
Gradient
The collection of derivatives of the loss with respect to every weight: for each weight, the rate at
which the loss would change if that weight changed. It is what tells training which direction to
move each weight.
Chain rule
The rule of calculus for differentiating a composition of functions, which is what makes it possible
to compute the gradient of a loss with respect to a weight many layers away from it.
430

Handwriting Robot Code theory DemoCode edition
Backpropagation
Applying the chain rule layer by layer from the loss back to the first layer, so that every weight’s
gradient is obtained in one backward pass.
Forward pass, backward pass
Computing the output from the input, and computing the gradients from the loss, respectively.
Batch
A group of examples processed together, so that one weight update is based on their average
gradient rather than on a single example, which is both faster and less noisy.
Epoch
One complete pass through the training data.
Learning rate
How far each weight is moved per update.
Optimiser
The rule that turns gradients into weight updates.
Overfitting
Learning the training examples rather than the general pattern, so that performance on new data
is poor. It is detected by measuring on data the network was not trained on.
Holdout, or validation set
Data deliberately excluded from training and kept for measurement, which is the only way an
accuracy figure means anything.
Checkpoint
A saved copy of all the weights, so a trained network can be reloaded later.
Recurrent layer
A layer that processes a sequence one position at a time while carrying information forward, so
that a decision at one position can depend on earlier ones.
Inference
Running a trained network forward to get an answer, as opposed to training it.
18.4 This project’s own terms
Glyph
One stored example of one character in one writer’s hand: a set of pen strokes, in x-height units,
with measurements describing how much space it occupies.
Variant
One of several stored glyphs for the same character by the same writer, since nobody writes a
letter identically twice.
Prior distance
A number measuring how far a stored glyph’s shape sits from the typical shape of that character
pooled across all writers. Low means a well-formed letter; high means the shape was probably cut
out wrongly.
Anchor, or fallback letterform
A clean, readable shape used in place of a stored variant when the stored variants are too damaged
to be legible. Preferably the writer’s own most typical version of the letter.
431

Handwriting Robot Code theory DemoCode edition
Legibility lambda
A number between 0 and 1 controlling how often the anchor is used in place of the writer’s own
shapes, and therefore where the output sits between being readable and being recognisably that
person’s hand.
Connectedness
The measured fraction of neighbouring letter pairs within a word that the writer joins without
lifting the pen.
Ligature
The joining stroke between two letters written without lifting the pen.
Trajectory
The pipeline’s representation of a drawing: a list of pen strokes in millimetres.
G-code
The text format understood by the machine, consisting of lines such asG1 X10 Y20 F900 , meaning
“move in a straight line to this position at this feed rate”.
Endstop
A switch at the end of an axis’s travel, used to find a known position and to prevent the machine
driving into its own frame.
